canton-of-cartagena.t: The most durable of the 1873 Spanish cantons, which seized the navy's main base and held out for six months against the Republic.
canton-of-cartagena.o: On 12 July 1873 intransigent federalists led by Antonio Gálvez Arce, known as Antoñete, proclaimed the Canton of Cartagena. They seized the naval arsenal and much of the Mediterranean fleet, and a revolutionary junta called on other cities to join a Cantonal Federation.
canton-of-cartagena.r: The canton issued its own coins and newspaper and used the fleet, commanded by General Juan Contreras, to raid Alicante, Almería and other ports for supplies. Foreign powers declared its ships pirates. Its leaders saw it as the seed of a federal Spain.
canton-of-cartagena.e: Government forces besieged Cartagena from the autumn of 1873. Weakened by bombardment and the explosion of its arsenal, it surrendered on 12 January 1874, and many leaders escaped to French Algeria. The rebellion helped discredit the Spanish First Republic.

cantabri.t: The mountain people of northern Spain whose resistance in the Cantabrian Wars of 29 to 19 BCE brought Augustus himself to Iberia.
cantabri.o: The Cantabri lived in the Cantabrian mountains and coast of northern Spain, in modern Cantabria and parts of Burgos, Palencia and León, from about the 4th century BCE. They were a Celtic-speaking people organised in clans, living in hillforts.
cantabri.r: Their mountain economy was based on herding goats and cattle, acorn bread and limited farming, and Strabo noted customs in which daughters inherited and husbands brought dowries. Their warriors raided the plains and served as mercenaries; their cavalry manoeuvre, the Cantabrian circle, was adopted by the Romans. They were never united under a single ruler.
cantabri.e: Augustus opened the Cantabrian Wars in 29 BCE, campaigning in person in 26 BCE, but conquest was completed only by Agrippa in 19 BCE, after mass deportations. The land became part of Hispania Tarraconensis; the name later reappeared in the Duchy of Cantabria.

commune-of-vercelli.t: A Piedmontese city-republic on the road to France that founded one of Italy's earliest universities in 1228.
commune-of-vercelli.o: Vercelli's powerful bishops held comital rights over the city, but citizens governed through consuls by around 1120. The commune expanded across the plain of the Sesia, competing with Novara, Casale and the March of Montferrat.
commune-of-vercelli.r: Consuls and later a podestà ran the commune, which joined the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa. In 1228 it agreed with students and masters from Padua to found a studium, one of the earliest Italian universities. Cardinal Guala Bicchieri, papal legate in England, founded the abbey of Sant'Andrea, a Gothic landmark begun in 1219. The rival Avogadro and Tizzoni families split the city.
commune-of-vercelli.e: In 1335 Vercelli accepted Azzone Visconti and became part of the Lordship of Milan. It passed to the County of Savoy in 1427.

county-of-montbeliard.t: A French-speaking Lutheran enclave ruled by the dukes of Württemberg for four centuries before France annexed it in 1793.
county-of-montbeliard.o: Montbéliard guarded the Belfort Gap between the Jura and the Vosges. Around 1042 Louis of Mousson, who also held Bar through his wife Sophie, ruled it as count. Later houses of Montfaucon and Chalon held it, all within the Kingdom of Arles and so in the Holy Roman Empire.
county-of-montbeliard.r: In 1397 the heiress Henriette of Montbéliard was betrothed to Eberhard IV of Württemberg, and the county passed to the Württemberg dynasty. From the 1520s, after preaching by Guillaume Farel, it became Lutheran, an unusual Protestant enclave between Catholic Franche-Comté and Alsace. Duke Frederick I ruled it from 1581 and brought in the architect Heinrich Schickhardt.
county-of-montbeliard.e: French troops occupied the county several times, and in 1793 the French First Republic annexed it. Württemberg recognised the loss in 1796. The region kept its Lutheran heritage and later became the home of the Peugeot industrial dynasty.

comtat-venaissin.t: A papal territory in Provence, governed from Carpentras for five centuries, where the popes lived at nearby Avignon in the 14th century.
comtat-venaissin.o: The Comtat had belonged to the counts of Toulouse. By the Treaty of Paris of 1229 after the Albigensian Crusade, Raymond VII ceded it to the Church, but the French crown held it until Philip III handed it to Pope Gregory X in 1274.
comtat-venaissin.r: The Comtat was governed by a papal rector at Carpentras, with its own estates. The papacy moved to neighbouring Avignon in 1309 and bought the city in 1348, and the region flourished during the Avignon papacy. Jews expelled from France found refuge there as the 'Pope's Jews', living in communities at Carpentras, Cavaillon, Avignon and L'Isle-sur-la-Sorgue.
comtat-venaissin.e: France occupied the territory several times in disputes with the popes. During the Revolution, after local votes, the National Constituent Assembly annexed Avignon and the Comtat to France in 1791; the papacy accepted the loss in the Treaty of Tolentino in 1797.

cerretani.t: The Pyrenean people of Cerdanya, famed in Roman times for their hams, whose name lives on in the Cerdanya valley.
cerretani.o: The Cerretani occupied the high Pyrenean valley of Cerdanya and the upper Segre, today divided between Spain, France and Andorra. They probably spoke an Iberian language, and are recorded from the late Iron Age.
cerretani.r: They lived from pastoralism and farming in the mountains, and Strabo noted that their hams were highly prized and profitable. Little is known of their political organisation. Their valley controlled routes across the Pyrenees between the Ebro basin and Gaul.
cerretani.e: They came under Roman control in the 2nd century BCE as part of Hispania Citerior. Pliny the Elder names the Roman town of Iulia Libica, modern Llívia, in their territory, and the name of the people survives in the region of Cerdanya.

commune-of-reggio.t: An Emilian city-republic between Parma and Modena that changed masters many times before passing finally to the Este in 1409.
commune-of-reggio.o: Reggio, on the Via Emilia, had consuls by 1136, after the citizens took power from the bishop and from the lords of the Canossa lands. The commune extended its control into the Apennine foothills.
commune-of-reggio.r: The commune was governed by consuls, then a podestà and popular councils, and joined the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa. Its position between larger neighbours made it a pawn: the Este held it from 1289 to 1306, and in the 14th century it passed among various lords, including the Gonzaga under Feltrino Gonzaga and then the Visconti. Factions of the Fogliani, Roberti and Canossa families divided the city.
commune-of-reggio.e: In 1409 Niccolò III d'Este acquired Reggio, which then remained an Este possession and part of the Duchy of Modena and Reggio until 1859. In 1797 it hosted the congress of the Cispadane Republic.

county-of-horne.t: A small county around Weert in the Maas valley, whose last notable count was beheaded with Egmont in Brussels in 1568.
county-of-horne.o: The lords of Horne held lands near Roermond and Weert from the 12th century as vassals in the region between Guelders, Brabant and Liège. Around 1450 Jacob I of Horne was raised to the rank of count, and the county became an imperial fief.
county-of-horne.r: Horne was a rural county of heath and farmland, with its castle at Horn and its main town at Weert. The counts served the Burgundian and Habsburg courts. Philip de Montmorency, count of Horne, an admiral and knight of the Golden Fleece, joined the noble opposition to Philip II's policies in the Netherlands.
county-of-horne.e: The Duke of Alba had Horne and Egmont beheaded in Brussels in 1568, a spark of the Dutch Revolt. The county passed to his relatives and in 1614 to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège; it is now divided between the Netherlands and Belgium.

carantania.t: An early Slavic principality in the eastern Alps, ancestor of Carinthia, famous for its unusual ceremony of installing dukes on the Prince's Stone.
carantania.o: Alpine Slavs settled the eastern Alps in the late 6th century under Avar overlordship. After Samo's death around 658 they formed an independent principality centred on the Zollfeld plain near Karnburg in modern Carinthia. A ruler named Valuk appears in Fredegar as 'duke of the Wends' around 631.
carantania.r: Around 743 Prince Borut sought Bavarian help against the Avars and accepted Bavarian overlordship; his son Gorazd and nephew Hotimir were raised as Christians, and Salzburg led the mission. Princes were installed on the Prince's Stone (Knežji kamen) in a ceremony led by peasants speaking Slavic, a rite later used for dukes of Carinthia.
carantania.e: After a pagan revolt in the 770s, Carantania passed with Bavaria under Frankish rule in 788. Following the uprising of Ljudevit Posavski, the native princes were replaced by Frankish counts in 828. The land became the core of the later Duchy of Carinthia and is a landmark in Slovene history.

county-of-girona.t: One of the first Frankish counties south of the Pyrenees, created when Girona surrendered to Charlemagne in 785.
county-of-girona.o: In 785 the people of Girona handed their city to Charlemagne's forces, and a county was set up under Frankish rule as part of the frontier that became the Marca Hispanica. Its first known count was Rostany.
county-of-girona.r: Counts appointed by the Carolingian kings governed Girona alongside its bishop, defending the frontier against al-Andalus. The county included the plain around the city and controlled the road from Gaul to Barcelona. It was often held together with Barcelona, and its counts were frequently Goths of local or Septimanian origin.
county-of-girona.e: From 878 Girona was held by Wilfred the Hairy with Barcelona and Osona. After his death in 897 it passed with Barcelona to his heirs and remained permanently part of the domains of the counts of Barcelona.

commune-of-prato.t: A Tuscan wool-making city-republic, home of the merchant Francesco Datini, which was sold to Florence in 1351.
commune-of-prato.o: Prato grew around the castle of the Alberti counts and the parish church of Santo Stefano, and consuls governed it by 1140. The commune developed in the shadow of Florence, a few miles away.
commune-of-prato.r: Prato was ruled by consuls and later a podestà, and its economy rested on wool cloth production, using the Bisenzio river to power fulling mills. The cathedral holds the relic of the Virgin's girdle, a major object of devotion. From the early 14th century the town placed itself under the Angevin kings of Naples to keep its independence from Florence.
commune-of-prato.e: In 1351 Queen Joanna I of Naples sold her rights over Prato to the Republic of Florence, which ruled it from then on. The merchant Francesco Datini, whose huge archive survives, later made his fortune there.

county-of-savoy.t: The Alpine county that controlled the Mont Cenis and Great St Bernard passes, the cradle of the house of Savoy and of later Italian kings.
county-of-savoy.o: Humbert White-Hands, a noble of the Kingdom of Arles, held counties around Maurienne and Savoy from around 1003. His son Odo married Adelaide of Turin, bringing lands in Piedmont, so the dynasty straddled the Alps from its beginnings.
county-of-savoy.r: The counts drew their power from controlling the main passes between France and Italy and from tolls on the trade that crossed them. Peter II, called the 'little Charlemagne', won the Vaud in the 13th century, and Chambéry became the capital in 1295. Amadeus VI, the Green Count, led a crusade in 1366, and Amadeus VII acquired Nice in 1388.
county-of-savoy.e: In 1416 Emperor Sigismund raised Amadeus VIII to the rank of duke, and the county became the Duchy of Savoy. The dynasty went on to rule Sardinia and, from 1861, all Italy.

costoboci.t: Dacian people north of the Carpathians whose daring raid of 170 CE reached Greece and sacked the sanctuary of Eleusis.
costoboci.o: Known mainly from Roman sources, the Costoboci were a Dacian people living beyond Roman Dacia, probably in the upper Dniester and Prut region of modern Ukraine and Romania, in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. An inscription in Rome names a Costobocian king, Pieporus.
costoboci.r: Little is known of their society beyond Roman notices. During the Marcomannic Wars, in about 170 CE, they broke through the Danube frontier, swept through Moesia, Thrace and Macedonia, and plundered the mysteries sanctuary at Eleusis near Athens.
costoboci.e: Soon after the raid they were attacked by the Asding Vandals, who took their lands. They vanish from the record by the end of the 2nd century, probably absorbed by the Carpi and other neighbours.

corsican-republic.t: Pasquale Paoli's independent Corsica, whose written constitution of 1755 made it one of the first modern republics and inspired admirers across Europe.
corsican-republic.o: After decades of rebellion against Genoa, the Corsican assembly elected Pasquale Paoli as General of the Nation in July 1755. In November he gave the island a constitution establishing a national assembly elected by male heads of family, with Corte as the capital.
corsican-republic.r: Paoli built a state from the interior, founding a university at Corte in 1765, a mint, a navy and the port of L'Île-Rousse. Justice was reformed to curb vendettas. James Boswell's Account of Corsica of 1768 made Paoli famous in Britain and among Enlightenment writers, but Genoa still held the main ports.
corsican-republic.e: In 1768, by the Treaty of Versailles, Genoa ceded its rights over Corsica to France. French troops defeated the Corsicans at Ponte Novu in May 1769, Paoli went into exile in Britain, and the island became part of the Kingdom of France.

cadurci.t: Gallic people of Quercy whose hill fort of Uxellodunum was the last stronghold to resist Caesar, in 51 BCE.
cadurci.o: The Cadurci lived in the valley of the Lot and its limestone plateaus, in the modern Lot. They were clients of the Arverni and produced linen famous in the Roman world.
cadurci.r: Their leader Lucterius was one of the most active commanders of the revolt of 52 BCE, raising peoples of the south to threaten the Roman Province.
cadurci.e: In 51 BCE Lucterius and the Senonian Drappes held Uxellodunum, probably the Puy d'Issolud. Caesar cut off its water supply by tunnelling to the spring, and after the surrender he cut off the hands of the defenders as a warning. Under Rome their town Divona became Cahors.

curonians.t: Seafaring Baltic people of the coast of Courland, feared as pirates across the Baltic, who resisted the Livonian crusade until 1267.
curonians.o: The Curonians lived along the Baltic coast of what is now western Latvia and Lithuania. Rimbert's life of Ansgar describes a Swedish king attacking their stronghold at Apuolė in 854, and they appear in Norse sagas as both trading partners and raiders. Their land was divided into several districts, each with its own hillforts and leaders.
curonians.r: They combined farming and fishing with seaborne trade and plunder, raiding Danish and Swedish coasts in the 11th to 13th centuries. Their cremation burials and weapons resemble those of Scandinavians. In 1230 a ruler called Lamekins made a treaty with the papal legate Baldwin of Alna, accepting baptism in return for keeping his lands.
curonians.e: The Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Courland conquered them between 1240 and 1267, despite a great uprising after the Order's defeat at Durbe in 1260. Many Curonian freemen kept a special status as 'Curonian kings' into modern times, and the people merged into the Latvians and Lithuanians.

county-of-coimbra.t: A frontier county of the Kingdom of Asturias and León created when Christian forces took Coimbra in 878, lost to Almanzor in 987.
county-of-coimbra.o: In 878 Hermenegildo Gutiérrez, a noble serving Alfonso III of Asturias, captured Coimbra on the Mondego from the Emirate of Córdoba. The city became the centre of a frontier county stretching south from the Douro, settled by northern Christians and local Mozarabs.
county-of-coimbra.r: The counts were military governors for the Asturian and Leonese kings, defending a vulnerable frontier and organising resettlement. Mozarabic Christians from al-Andalus brought Arabic culture and Visigothic church traditions, and monasteries such as Lorvão became important landowners. Power passed among a few noble families who intermarried with the counts of Portugal.
county-of-coimbra.e: In 987 Almanzor captured Coimbra, ending the county; the city was left largely deserted for a time. Ferdinand I of León retook it in 1064, and in 1096 it was joined to the County of Portugal, later becoming the first capital of the Kingdom of Portugal.

county-of-osona.t: The Catalan county of the plain of Vic, resettled by Wilfred the Hairy, where the monasteries of Ripoll and Vic grew into centres of learning.
county-of-osona.o: Osona, named after the ancient Ausetani, came under Frankish rule around 798. After the revolt of Aissó in 826 it was largely abandoned. From about 879 Wilfred the Hairy repopulated the plain of Vic, restored its bishopric in 886 and founded the monasteries of Ripoll and Sant Joan de les Abadesses.
county-of-osona.r: Osona was a frontier county facing al-Andalus, settled by free peasant colonists who cleared land and built castles. It was usually held by the counts of Barcelona rather than having its own line. Its church centres flourished: Ripoll's library made it a hub of learning in the 10th century, where Gerbert of Aurillac studied Arabic science.
county-of-osona.e: Osona remained in the hands of the House of Barcelona, briefly granted to younger sons, until it was fully merged with the County of Barcelona. It became part of Catalonia and the Crown of Aragon, and Vic remains its centre.

county-of-forcalquier.t: A county of upper Provence that broke away from the main comital line and was reunited with Provence in 1209.
county-of-forcalquier.o: The county arose from the division of the inheritance of the counts of Provence in the mid-11th century, when one branch kept rights in the north-east around Forcalquier, Sisteron and the Durance valley. In the 12th century it passed to the counts of Urgell, who ruled it as a separate principality.
county-of-forcalquier.r: Forcalquier was a land of hill towns and pasture along the Durance, controlling routes between Provence and the Alps. Count William IV, the most prominent ruler, held out against the Catalan counts of Provence and the emperors for decades.
county-of-forcalquier.e: In 1193 William IV's granddaughter Garsenda married Alfonso II of Provence, and on William's death in 1209 Forcalquier was reunited with the County of Provence. Their son Raymond Berengar IV ruled both.

county-of-toulouse.t: Great southern principality, heart of Occitan culture and troubadour poetry, destroyed by the Albigensian Crusade.
county-of-toulouse.o: Charlemagne appointed Chorson count of Toulouse in 778, followed by William of Gellone, later a saint. In the 9th century the county passed to a hereditary line known as the Raymondines, who extended their power over Rouergue, Quercy, Albi and parts of Languedoc and Provence.
county-of-toulouse.r: The counts ruled a loosely held territory of powerful vassals and self-governing towns, where Toulouse was run by elected consuls. Count Raymond IV led a great army on the First Crusade and founded the County of Tripoli. The court fostered troubadour poetry, and the Cathar heresy spread widely in its lands.
county-of-toulouse.e: The Albigensian Crusade from 1209 brought northern French armies under Simon de Montfort, who defeated Raymond VI and Peter II of Aragon at Muret in 1213. By the Treaty of Paris in 1229 Raymond VII's heiress Joan married Alphonse of Poitiers, and on their deaths in 1271 the county passed to the Kingdom of France.

chalcidian-league.t: Federation of the Greek towns of Chalcidice centred on Olynthus, the strongest power of the northern Aegean until Philip II of Macedon destroyed it.
chalcidian-league.o: In 432 BCE the Chalcidian towns, persuaded by Perdiccas II of Macedon, revolted from the Delian League, and many of their people moved into Olynthus. From this union grew a federal state calling itself 'the Chalcidians'. With help from the Spartan Brasidas in 424 BCE it secured its independence from Athens.
chalcidian-league.r: Member towns shared citizenship, laws on marriage and property and a common silver coinage showing Apollo and his lyre, among the finest of the age. In the early 4th century BCE the league grew aggressively, absorbing Potidaea and even occupying Pella, the Macedonian capital, during the troubles of Amyntas III.
chalcidian-league.e: Appeals from Acanthus and Apollonia brought a Spartan war (382-379 BCE) that forced the league to dissolve. It revived, allied first with Philip II and then with Athens, but Philip besieged Olynthus and destroyed it in 348 BCE, ending the league and annexing Chalcidice to Macedon.

cananefates.t: Germanic people of the Dutch coast near The Hague, kin of the Batavi, who joined the Batavian revolt of 69 CE.
cananefates.o: Tacitus says the Cananefates were related to the Batavi and equal to them in origin, language and courage, though fewer in number. They lived in the coastal dunes and peat lands of the western Netherlands, between the Rhine mouth and the sea.
cananefates.r: Like the Batavi they supplied soldiers to Rome, including cavalry units. Tacitus describes how in 69 CE they chose Brinno as their leader by raising him on a shield, the earliest recorded example of this Germanic custom.
cananefates.e: Under Brinno they attacked Roman forts on the coast at the start of the revolt of Julius Civilis. After its defeat they returned to Roman rule, and their chief town became Forum Hadriani (Voorburg), granted market rights under Hadrian. Frankish raids in the 3rd century ended Roman life there.

county-of-flanders.t: Rich medieval county on the North Sea whose cloth towns of Bruges, Ghent and Ypres made it one of the wealthiest regions of Europe.
county-of-flanders.o: In 862 Baldwin I, called Iron Arm, eloped with Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, and was given lands around Bruges to defend against the Vikings. His descendants expanded the county from the Scheldt to the Canche, holding most of it as vassals of the Kingdom of France and a smaller part, Imperial Flanders, from the Holy Roman Empire.
county-of-flanders.r: Flanders grew rich on weaving English wool into fine cloth, and its towns gained wide self-government and often defied the counts and the French kings. Count Baldwin IX became the first Latin emperor of Constantinople in 1204. In 1302 Flemish townsmen defeated French knights at the Battle of the Golden Spurs at Courtrai.
county-of-flanders.e: In 1384 Flanders passed to Philip the Bold of Burgundy and became part of the Burgundian State, then of the Habsburg Netherlands and the Spanish Netherlands. France conquered its southern part in the 17th century, and the rest was annexed by France in 1795.

contestani.t: The Iberian people of Alicante and Murcia whose sculptors produced the Lady of Elche, the masterpiece of Iberian art.
contestani.o: The Contestani occupied the coast and hinterland of south-east Spain, roughly the modern provinces of Alicante and parts of Murcia and Valencia, from the 5th century BCE. They grew out of earlier Iberian communities in close contact with Phoenician and Greek traders.
contestani.r: Their towns, such as Ilici (La Alcudia, Elche), La Serreta near Alcoy and Lucentum, were centres of a refined Iberian culture. The stone bust of the Lady of Elche, carved around the 4th century BCE, comes from their territory. They wrote their Iberian language in a Greek-derived alphabet, recorded on lead tablets, and traded olive oil, wine and esparto.
contestani.e: After Carthaginian control under Barcid Iberia, the region passed to Rome when Scipio captured Carthago Nova in 209 BCE, and was pacified by 197 BCE. Ilici became a Roman colony, and the Contestani merged into Hispania Citerior.

county-of-champagne.t: The county of the great Champagne fairs, where Flemish cloth met Italian merchants and the court of Troyes nurtured Chrétien de Troyes.
county-of-champagne.o: The counties of Troyes and Meaux were built up in the 10th century by Herbert the Old of Vermandois and passed around 1022 to Odo II of Blois. A younger branch of the Blois family took Troyes, and Count Hugh was styled count of Champagne by around 1102. Theobald II reunited Blois and Champagne in the 12th century.
county-of-champagne.r: The counts protected the cycle of fairs at Troyes, Provins, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube, which made Champagne the commercial crossroads of 12th- and 13th-century Europe. Henry the Liberal and Marie de Champagne made Troyes a literary centre, home of Chrétien de Troyes. Count Theobald IV, a trouvère poet, became king of Navarre in 1234.
county-of-champagne.e: Countess Joan I married Philip IV in 1284, and when their son Louis X became king in 1314, Champagne passed into the royal domain of the Kingdom of France. The fairs had already declined as sea routes to Flanders opened.

county-of-konigsegg.t: Upper Swabian county of the Königsegg family, imperial counts who served the Habsburgs as soldiers and diplomats.
county-of-konigsegg.o: The Königsegg family, Swabian ministerials named after a castle near Saulgau, accumulated lordships around Aulendorf and in the Allgäu. In 1629 they were raised to imperial counts, and the lands were divided between the lines of Königsegg-Aulendorf and Königsegg-Rothenfels, the latter centred on Immenstadt.
county-of-konigsegg.r: The counties were small Catholic territories held within the Swabian Circle, administered from Aulendorf Castle. Members of the family pursued careers in Habsburg service: Lothar Joseph Dominik von Königsegg-Rothenfels was an imperial field marshal and diplomat, and Maximilian Friedrich von Königsegg-Rothenfels became archbishop-elector of Cologne in 1761.
county-of-konigsegg.e: Königsegg-Rothenfels was exchanged with Austria for estates in Hungary in 1804. Königsegg-Aulendorf was mediatised in 1806 and placed under the Kingdom of Württemberg, the family keeping its estates and castle.

county-of-poitou.t: County centred on Poitiers whose counts became dukes of Aquitaine and passed their lands to Eleanor of Aquitaine and the Plantagenets.
county-of-poitou.o: Carolingian counts ruled Poitiers from the late 8th century. In the 9th century the Ramnulfid family made the office hereditary, and in the 10th century Count William III, called Towhead, took the title of Duke of Aquitaine, after which the two titles were held together.
county-of-poitou.r: The counts ruled from Poitiers over a land of abbeys, castles and salt-producing coasts. Duke William IX, the first known troubadour, wrote poetry in Occitan, and his granddaughter Eleanor of Aquitaine carried the county first to Louis VII of the Kingdom of France and then to Henry II of England.
county-of-poitou.e: Philip II seized Poitou from King John from 1204, and Louis VIII completed the conquest in 1224. It became an appanage for Alphonse of Poitiers and later for John, Duke of Berry, on whose death in 1416 it returned to the crown.

commune-of-lodi.t: A Lombard city-republic refounded on a new site by Frederick Barbarossa in 1158 after Milan had destroyed the old town.
commune-of-lodi.o: Milan destroyed the old town of Lodi in 1111 and again in 1158. That year Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, whom the Lodigiani had appealed to, refounded the city on a new site on the Adda, a few miles from the old one, now Lodi Vecchio. The new commune grew under imperial protection.
commune-of-lodi.r: The commune was governed by consuls and later a podestà. Although founded as an imperial ally, Lodi joined the Lombard League in 1167. The cathedral was begun in the year of its refoundation. The town lived from farming and river trade, but was always overshadowed by Milan. In the 13th and 14th centuries the Fissiraga and Vistarini families competed for control.
commune-of-lodi.e: In 1335 Lodi submitted to Azzone Visconti and became part of the Lordship of Milan. The Peace of Lodi of 1454 between Milan and Venice was later signed there.

chalcis.t: Euboean city on the Euripus strait that pioneered Greek colonisation in Italy, Sicily and the Chalcidice and spread its alphabet to the Etruscans and Romans.
chalcis.o: Chalcis grew on the narrowest point of the Euripus channel between Euboea and mainland Greece. Ionian in dialect, it was an early trading power by the 8th century BCE. Its long rivalry with nearby Eretria for the Lelantine plain, the Lelantine War, drew in allies from much of Greece.
chalcis.r: With Eretria, Chalcidians founded Pithekoussai and Cumae in Italy; alone they founded Naxos, Leontini and Catana in Sicily, Rhegium and many towns in the Chalcidice. Their version of the alphabet passed to the Etruscans and Latins. Chalcis was governed by a landowning aristocracy, the hippobotai, or horse-breeders.
chalcis.e: Athens defeated Chalcis in 506 BCE and settled colonists on its land. After revolts against the Delian League it became a Macedonian stronghold, one of the 'fetters of Greece', and Aristotle died there in 322 BCE. Rome sacked it in 146 BCE for joining the Achaean League's war.

cauci.t: People of Ireland's east coast recorded only in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography, whose name echoes the Chauci of northern Germany.
cauci.o: The Cauci are known solely from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which drew on earlier reports by merchants and sailors. He places them on the east coast of Ireland, between the Eblani to the north and the Manapii to the south, roughly in the area of modern Dublin and Wicklow.
cauci.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or way of life. Their name closely resembles that of the Chauci, a Germanic people of the North Sea coast, which has prompted speculation about settlers or traders from the Continent, but most scholars treat the likeness as coincidence or a copying error.
cauci.e: No later source mentions them, and Irish tradition preserves no matching name. Their region later formed part of the Kingdom of Leinster.

county-of-nice.t: The Riviera county that chose Savoy over Provence in 1388, gave the Savoyards their outlet to the sea and passed to France in 1860.
county-of-nice.o: During the war of succession that followed Queen Joanna I's death, Nice and its hinterland rejected the Angevin claimant and in 1388, in the act known as the Dedition, placed themselves under Amadeus VII of Savoy. Nice thus left the County of Provence and became Savoy's outlet to the Mediterranean.
county-of-nice.r: The county was governed by Savoyard officials and later a senate at Nice, with Villefranche as the dukes' naval base. In 1543 a Franco-Ottoman fleet besieged Nice, an event remembered through the heroine Catherine Ségurane. The people spoke Niçard Occitan, while Italian was the language of administration. Giuseppe Garibaldi was born there in 1807.
county-of-nice.e: France occupied Nice from 1792 to 1814. Under the Treaty of Turin of 1860, Victor Emmanuel II ceded it to Napoleon III's Second French Empire in return for help in Italian unification, ratified by a plebiscite.

county-of-ponthieu.t: A small county at the mouth of the Somme where Harold Godwinson was held captive and where the English won at Crécy.
county-of-ponthieu.o: Ponthieu emerged around 980 when Hugh, a castellan of Abbeville, married a daughter of Hugh Capet and was recognised as count. Abbeville became the seat of a modest dynasty on the coast between Normandy and Flanders.
county-of-ponthieu.r: The counts profited from the Somme estuary and the cloth and salt trades. In 1064 Count Guy I captured the shipwrecked Harold Godwinson and handed him to William of Normandy, as shown on the Bayeux Tapestry. In 1279 the county passed through Eleanor of Castile to her husband Edward I of England.
county-of-ponthieu.e: The English kings held Ponthieu as vassals of France; Edward III fought at Crécy, inside the county, in 1346, and the Treaty of Brétigny of 1360 gave it to him in full sovereignty. French forces reconquered it in 1369, and it joined the Kingdom of France, later passing briefly to Burgundy.

county-of-novellara.t: A tiny Emilian county ruled for over three centuries by a cadet branch of the Gonzaga family.
county-of-novellara.o: After losing the lordship of Reggio in 1371, Feltrino Gonzaga, of the family that ruled Mantua, kept the small territory of Novellara and Bagnolo in the plain north of Reggio. His descendants ruled it as an imperial fief, later recognised as a county.
county-of-novellara.r: The counts of Novellara governed a few villages and a fortified town from their castle, the Rocca. They lived from farming the rich plain and from service at larger courts, and maintained a modest Renaissance court; the painter Lelio Orsi worked for them in the 16th century. The state survived by careful loyalty to the emperors and good relations with the Este and Gonzaga.
county-of-novellara.e: The line of Gonzaga-Novellara died out in 1728. After disputes over the succession, the emperor granted the county to Rinaldo d'Este in 1737, and it became part of the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

cortona.t: Etruscan hill city above the Val di Chiana, known for its monumental tumuli and the Tabula Cortonensis, one of the longest Etruscan texts.
cortona.o: Cortona, Etruscan Curtun, sits high on a spur of Monte Sant'Egidio overlooking the Val di Chiana and Lake Trasimeno. Greek and Roman writers credited it with legendary origins, linking it to Dardanus or to Pelasgian settlers. Archaeologically it developed into a city in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, when its first walls were built.
cortona.r: Cortona's elite built the great 'Melone' tumuli at Sodo below the town, one with a monumental stepped altar decorated with sphinxes devouring warriors. Its bronzes include a famous hanging lamp with sixteen burners. The Tabula Cortonensis, a bronze tablet of about 200 BCE found in 1992, records a land transaction among named families and is a key source for the Etruscan language and law.
cortona.e: Livy names Cortona with Perusia and Arretium among the cities that made a thirty-year truce with Rome in 310 BCE. It gradually became a Roman ally and later a municipium, overshadowed by Arretium. The Etruscan walls still underlie the medieval town.

cassi.t: British people named only by Julius Caesar in 54 BCE, sometimes linked by name with Cassivellaunus, leader of resistance to Rome.
cassi.o: The Cassi are recorded once in Caesar's Gallic War as one of five British peoples, with the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Ancalites and Bibroci, who sent envoys to surrender during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
cassi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Because their name resembles that of Cassivellaunus, some historians suggest they were his own people or a group within his following north of the Thames, perhaps in Hertfordshire, but there is no firm evidence.
cassi.e: They do not appear again in any source. Their territory, wherever it lay, was absorbed into larger polities such as the Catuvellauni before the Roman conquest of 43.

cornavii-caithness.t: People of Caithness at the northern tip of mainland Britain, recorded by Ptolemy and named after their headlands.
cornavii-caithness.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Cornavii in the far north-east of mainland Scotland, in modern Caithness. Their name, from a Celtic word for horn, probably means 'people of the promontory', referring to headlands such as Duncansby Head or Dunnet Head; the same name was borne by the Cornovii of the English Midlands and by the people of Cornwall.
cornavii-caithness.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Caithness has one of the densest concentrations of brochs in Scotland, tall drystone towers built in the last centuries BCE, which point to a society of powerful local families controlling fertile farmland and coastal resources.
cornavii-caithness.e: The Cornavii do not appear after Ptolemy. Caithness later formed part of the lands of the northern Picts before falling under Norse rule as part of the earldom of Orkney in the 9th and 10th centuries.

cumae.t: The oldest Greek colony on the Italian mainland, home of the Sibyl, which passed the Greek alphabet to the Etruscans and Latins.
cumae.o: Euboean Greeks from Chalcis and Eretria founded Cumae around 740 BCE on the Campanian coast north of the Bay of Naples, having first settled the island of Pithekoussai (Ischia). The site, a steep acropolis above the sea, controlled the fertile Phlegraean Fields and gave access to Etruscan and native trade.
cumae.r: Cumae was an aristocratic city that became a major power in the Tyrrhenian world. Its version of the Greek alphabet was adopted by the Etruscans and, through them, by Rome. The cave of the Sibyl and the temple of Apollo made it a famous oracle. The tyrant Aristodemus defeated the Etruscans at Aricia around 504 BCE, and in 474 BCE Cumae and Hieron I of Syracuse destroyed an Etruscan fleet off the city. Cumae also founded Neapolis.
cumae.e: Around 421 BCE Samnite-speaking Campanians captured Cumae, and it became an Oscan town. It received Roman citizenship without the vote in 338 BCE, later became a Roman municipium and declined as nearby Puteoli grew. A Byzantine fortress in the 6th century CE, it was finally destroyed by Naples in 1207.

commune-of-parma.t: An Emilian city-republic that defeated Emperor Frederick II's siege in 1248 and commissioned Benedetto Antelami's great baptistery.
commune-of-parma.o: Parma's citizens gradually took power from their bishops, who had been counts of the city, and by 1149 consuls governed the commune. It controlled the Via Emilia and a route across the Apennines to Tuscany.
commune-of-parma.r: Governed by consuls, then a podestà and popular councils, Parma joined the Lombard League. In 1196 Benedetto Antelami began its octagonal baptistery. Ghibelline at first, it turned Guelph in 1247 and withstood Frederick II's siege, destroying his camp-city of Victoria in February 1248. The Rossi, Correggio and Sanvitale families competed for power; Giberto da Correggio became lord in 1303.
commune-of-parma.e: After a succession of lords, Obizzo III d'Este sold the city to Luchino Visconti in 1346, and it joined the Lordship of Milan. In 1545 it became the capital of the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza.

commune-of-milan.t: The leading city-republic of Lombardy, razed by Frederick Barbarossa in 1162 and then at the head of the league that defeated him at Legnano.
commune-of-milan.o: Milan's archbishops had long dominated the city, but by 1097 consuls drawn from nobles and citizens were governing it. The young commune extended its power over the surrounding countryside and over neighbours such as Lodi and Como, whose complaints drew Emperor Frederick Barbarossa into Italy.
commune-of-milan.r: Government passed from consuls to a podestà, usually an outsider, alongside councils and the popular credenza di Sant'Ambrogio. Milan was a manufacturing centre for wool cloth and arms, with its own Ambrosian liturgy. Barbarossa destroyed the city in 1162, but it was rebuilt, joined the Lombard League and helped defeat the emperor at Legnano in 1176, winning self-government at the Peace of Constance in 1183.
commune-of-milan.e: Rivalry between nobles and the popular party opened the way to strongmen. In 1259 Martino della Torre was made lord of the people, and the commune gave way to the Lordship of Milan, later dominated by the Visconti.

carolingian-kingdom-of-italy.t: The former Lombard kingdom under Charlemagne's dynasty, which made Italy part of the Frankish world and linked its crown to the imperial title.
carolingian-kingdom-of-italy.o: Charlemagne conquered the Lombard Kingdom in 774 and took the title King of the Lombards. In 781 Pope Hadrian I crowned his young son Pepin King of Italy, creating a subordinate kingdom with its capital at Pavia, covering northern and central Italy apart from Venice and the papal lands.
carolingian-kingdom-of-italy.r: The Carolingians kept Lombard law and the palace at Pavia but installed Frankish counts and bishops, issued capitularies for Italy and supported monasteries such as Bobbio and Nonantola. Pepin's son Bernard rebelled and was blinded in 817. Lothair I and his son Louis II ruled Italy as emperors; Louis II spent decades fighting Arab raiders in the south and recovered Bari in 871.
carolingian-kingdom-of-italy.e: After Louis II died in 875, the crown passed among Charles the Bald, Carloman and Charles the Fat, who was deposed in 887 and died in 888. Italian nobles then chose their own kings, beginning with Berengar of Friuli, and the Kingdom of Italy continued under them.

croton.t: Achaean Greek city of southern Italy famed for its athletes, its doctors and Pythagoras, which destroyed Sybaris in 510 BCE.
croton.o: Achaean colonists led by Myscellus of Rhypes founded Croton around 710 BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, reportedly on the advice of the Delphic oracle. It had a good harbour and a broad territory, and became one of the major powers of Magna Graecia.
croton.r: Croton produced more Olympic victors than any other city in some periods, above all the wrestler Milo. It was renowned for medicine, with Democedes and Alcmaeon. Around 530 BCE Pythagoras settled there, and his followers dominated politics for a time before being violently overthrown. The sanctuary of Hera Lacinia at Capo Colonna was a religious centre for the Italiote Greeks. After defeat by Locri at the Sagras river, Croton crushed Sybaris in 510 BCE.
croton.e: In the 4th century Croton suffered from Dionysius I, who held it from 379 BCE, and from the Bruttians and Agathocles. During the war with Pyrrhus it was taken by Rome in 277 BCE. A Roman colony was founded there in 194 BCE, and the town survives as Crotone.

cornouaille.t: Breton kingdom of south-western Brittany, founded by settlers from Britain and centred on Quimper.
cornouaille.o: From the 5th and 6th centuries migrants from western Britain settled the Armorican peninsula, once the land of the Osismii. Those in the south-west named their territory after Cornwall: Kernev in Breton, Cornubia in Latin. Its early history is known mainly from saints' lives and legends, such as that of King Gradlon and the drowned city of Ys.
cornouaille.r: The kingdom was ruled by local Breton dynasties and organised around monasteries and the see of Quimper, traditionally founded by Saint Corentin. The abbey of Landévennec, founded by Saint Guénolé, was its chief religious centre and produced important manuscripts.
cornouaille.e: In the 9th century Cornouaille was drawn into the unified Kingdom of Brittany under Nominoe and Erispoe. It survived as a county whose counts later became dukes of Brittany in the 11th century, and the name remains in use for the region around Quimper.

capua.t: The great city of Campania, Etruscan in origin and later Oscan, whose defection to Hannibal in 216 BCE ended in harsh Roman punishment.
capua.o: Capua lay in the fertile Campanian plain near the Volturno, on the site of modern Santa Maria Capua Vetere. The Etruscans developed it into a city in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE as the centre of their Campanian holdings. Around 423 BCE Oscan-speaking Samnites seized it, and its people became known as Campani.
capua.r: Capua grew rich on grain, wine, bronze-working and perfumes, and Romans saw it as a centre of luxury. It was governed by a chief magistrate, the meddix tuticus, and a senate. Threatened by the Samnites, it appealed to Rome in 343 BCE, triggering the First Samnite War, and from 338 BCE its citizens held Roman citizenship without the vote. Its Mother Goddess sanctuary yielded hundreds of stone statues of women with infants.
capua.e: After Cannae in 216 BCE Capua went over to Hannibal. Rome besieged it and took it in 211 BCE, executed its leaders, confiscated its land and abolished its self-government. It recovered as a Roman colony and later saw the slave revolt of Spartacus begin in its gladiator school in 73 BCE.

county-of-sicily.t: The Norman county that conquered Muslim Sicily and built the multilingual, multi-faith government later inherited by the Kingdom of Sicily.
county-of-sicily.o: Roger de Hauteville, Robert Guiscard's youngest brother, crossed to Sicily in 1061 and took Messina. With Guiscard he besieged Palermo, which fell in early 1072, and Roger became count of Sicily under his brother's overlordship. The conquest of the Emirate of Sicily took thirty years, ending with the fall of Noto in 1091, the year Roger also raided Malta.
county-of-sicily.r: Roger ruled a largely Muslim and Greek population with a thin Norman elite. He kept Arabic-speaking fiscal offices, recruited Muslim troops, refounded Latin bishoprics and endowed Greek monasteries. In 1098 Pope Urban II granted him unusual control over the Sicilian church. After his death in 1101, his widow Adelaide del Vasto ruled as regent and moved the court to Palermo.
county-of-sicily.e: Roger II came of age in 1112, absorbed the mainland Duchy of Apulia and Calabria in 1127 and was crowned king at Palermo on Christmas Day 1130. The county thus became the core of the Kingdom of Sicily.
county-of-sicily.re: Catholic Christianity, with Greek Orthodox Christianity and Sunni Islam
county-of-sicily.la: Arabic, Greek, Latin, Old Norman French

county-of-urgell.t: The longest-lasting Catalan county, ruled by the Ermengol counts from Balaguer, whose bishops became co-princes of Andorra.
county-of-urgell.o: Urgell, in the upper Segre valley, was taken by the Franks around 798 and organised as a county of the Marca Hispanica, often joined with Cerdanya. Wilfred the Hairy ruled it from 870. In 992 it passed to Ermengol I, son of Borrell II of Barcelona, founding a dynasty that lasted over two centuries.
county-of-urgell.r: The counts of Urgell, nearly all named Ermengol, pushed south against al-Andalus and conquered Balaguer in 1105, making it their capital. The bishops of La Seu d'Urgell held great influence, and an agreement of 1278 with the counts of Foix made them co-lords of Andorra. Later the county passed to a branch of the royal House of Barcelona.
county-of-urgell.e: Count James II claimed the throne of Aragon in 1410, but the Compromise of Caspe of 1412 chose Ferdinand of Antequera. James rebelled, was besieged in Balaguer in 1413 and imprisoned, and the county was confiscated. The bishop of Urgell remains co-prince of Andorra.

canton-of-cadiz.t: A revolutionary canton proclaimed in the port city of Cádiz in July 1873, one of the first to be crushed by the Republic's army.
canton-of-cadiz.o: In July 1873 the federalists of Cádiz, a city with strong radical and republican traditions, declared a sovereign canton as part of the Cantonal Rebellion against the central government of the Spanish First Republic.
canton-of-cadiz.r: A revolutionary committee governed the city and its militias, but it had little support beyond Cádiz itself and almost no time to organise.
canton-of-cadiz.e: After crushing the Canton of Seville, General Manuel Pavía advanced on Cádiz, which submitted in early August 1873 with little resistance.

cessetani.t: The Iberian people of the Tarragona area, near whose town Kese the Romans won their first battle in Iberia in 218 BCE.
cessetani.o: The Cessetani, or Cosetani, inhabited the Camp de Tarragona and the lower Penedès in southern Catalonia from about the 5th century BCE. Their main settlement was Kese, usually located at or near Tarragona.
cessetani.r: Their territory had fortified settlements such as Alorda Park at Calafell and lived from farming and trade along the coast. Kese minted widely circulated coins with an Iberian legend. Their political structure is not recorded, but they were prosperous enough for both Carthage and Rome to value the area.
cessetani.e: In 218 BCE Gnaeus Scipio defeated the Carthaginian commander Hanno near Cissa, and the Romans established their base at Tarraco. The region thus became Rome's first foothold in Iberia, and Tarraco grew into the capital of Hispania Citerior and later Tarraconensis.

county-of-luxembourg.t: The castle-county on the Alzette that gave the Holy Roman Empire three emperors and grew into the duchy behind today's Grand Duchy.
county-of-luxembourg.o: In 963 Count Siegfried acquired the rock of Lucilinburhuc from the abbey of St Maximin at Trier and built a castle there. His descendants, and from 1136 the counts of Namur and later Limburg lines, expanded the county through the Ardennes and Moselle valley.
county-of-luxembourg.r: Luxembourg was a bilingual land of German and French speakers. Count Henry VII became emperor in 1308, and his son John the Blind, king of Bohemia, died at Crécy in 1346. Emperor Charles IV raised the county to a duchy in 1354. The fortress city became one of Europe's strongest, later rebuilt by Vauban.
county-of-luxembourg.e: Elisabeth of Görlitz ceded the duchy to Philip the Good of the Burgundian State in 1443. It then passed with the Habsburg Netherlands to the Spanish Netherlands and Austrian Netherlands, was briefly French in 1684–1697, and was annexed by France in 1795. It was revived as the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in 1815.

commune-of-brescia.t: A combative Lombard city-republic, home of the reformer Arnold of Brescia, that withstood a siege by Emperor Frederick II in 1238.
commune-of-brescia.o: Brescia's citizens took power from their bishop in the late 11th and early 12th centuries, and the commune was governed by consuls by around 1100. It controlled a rich territory of valleys, iron mines and lakes between Lake Garda and Lake Iseo.
commune-of-brescia.r: The commune was run by consuls and later a podestà. The preacher Arnold of Brescia, who attacked clerical wealth, came from the city. Brescia joined the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa, resisted a long siege by Frederick II in 1238 and another by Henry VII in 1311. It was famed for iron working and arms making, and its Old Cathedral, the Rotonda, dates from this era.
commune-of-brescia.e: Exhausted by faction, Brescia accepted the Scaliger lords of Verona and then in 1337 submitted to Azzone Visconti, joining the Lordship of Milan. The Republic of Venice took it in 1426.

county-palatine-of-chester.t: A Norman marcher earldom on the Welsh border whose earls ruled Cheshire almost as independent princes.
county-palatine-of-chester.o: After crushing northern and Mercian resistance, William the Conqueror gave the earldom of Chester to Gerbod the Fleming and then, in 1071, to Hugh d'Avranches. Its purpose was to guard the northern Welsh border and push into Gwynedd.
county-palatine-of-chester.r: The earls held nearly all of Cheshire, with their own courts, sheriff and barons, and royal writs did not normally run there, a status later called palatine. Hugh and his cousin Robert of Rhuddlan advanced along the north Welsh coast. Ranulf de Gernon and Ranulf de Blondeville were major figures in the wars of Stephen and John; Ranulf III built Beeston Castle.
county-palatine-of-chester.e: When John the Scot, the last earl of the line, died childless in 1237, Henry III took the earldom into royal hands. From 1301 it was given to the heir to the throne, and Cheshire kept palatine institutions until 1830.

commune-of-bergamo.t: An Alpine-foothill city-republic in Lombardy, long torn between Guelph and Ghibelline clans before falling to Milan and then Venice.
commune-of-bergamo.o: Bergamo's bishops had held much of the city's authority, but consuls are recorded by 1098. The commune grew on wool, iron from the Bergamasque valleys and its position at the mouth of the Alpine valleys, and fought frequent border wars with Brescia.
commune-of-bergamo.r: Consuls and later a podestà governed with a large council. Bergamo joined the Lombard League in 1167 against Frederick Barbarossa, though it often leaned towards the emperors. In the 13th and 14th centuries the city was split between the Ghibelline Suardi and the Guelph Colleoni and Rivola families, whose feuds repeatedly invited outside lords into the upper town.
commune-of-bergamo.e: In 1332 Azzone Visconti took Bergamo into the Lordship of Milan. The Republic of Venice conquered it in 1428 and held it until 1797, when it briefly became the Republic of Bergamo.

county-of-blois.t: The Loire county of the Thibaudian counts, rivals of the early Capetians, whose family gave England King Stephen and later united with Champagne.
county-of-blois.o: Theobald the Trickster, a vassal of Hugh the Great, held Blois, Chartres and Tours by around 940 and founded a dynasty. His grandson Odo II added Troyes and Meaux around 1022, encircling the Capetian royal domain and contending with Anjou for Touraine, which was lost in 1044.
county-of-blois.r: The counts ruled a rich farming land of the Loire and the Beauce, with Chartres and its cathedral school a major centre of learning. Count Stephen-Henry, husband of Adela of Normandy, was a leader of the First Crusade, and their son Stephen became king of England in 1135. The family's Champagne branch, ruling the County of Champagne, became the more powerful line.
county-of-blois.e: From the 1230s the house of Châtillon held Blois. The last count, Guy II, sold it to Louis of Orléans in 1391, with possession at his death in 1397. When Louis's grandson, born at Blois, became Louis XII in 1498, it joined the Kingdom of France.

carpetani.t: A people of the central Meseta around Toledo and Madrid, defeated by Hannibal on the Tagus before Rome absorbed their lands.
carpetani.o: The Carpetani occupied the upper and middle Tagus basin, in modern Madrid, Toledo and Ciudad Real, from the second half of the first millennium BCE. Their language is thought to have been Celtic, though Iberian influences were strong.
carpetani.r: They lived in fortified towns such as Toletum and Complutum, on a farming and herding economy of the open plateau. Their political organisation is little known, but they could field large armies. In 220 BCE Hannibal defeated a coalition of Carpetani, Olcades and Vaccaei at the crossing of the Tagus.
carpetani.e: Rome reached their land in the early 2nd century BCE: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior took Toletum in 193 BCE, and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus pacified the region by 179 BCE. They became part of Hispania Citerior, and Toletum grew into Roman and later Visigothic Toledo.

crown-of-aragon.t: A composite Mediterranean monarchy uniting Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia and Majorca, whose rule stretched to Sicily, Sardinia, Naples and Athens.
crown-of-aragon.o: The marriage of Petronila of the Kingdom of Aragon and Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona united their lands, and their son Alfonso II inherited both in 1162. James I the Conqueror then took Majorca in 1229 and Valencia in 1238, creating the Kingdom of Majorca and the Kingdom of Valencia.
crown-of-aragon.r: The Crown was a federation: each realm kept its own laws, Cortes and currency under a shared king. Catalan merchants and naval power drove expansion, with Sicily won in 1282, Sardinia from 1323 and Naples in 1442. After the Compromise of Caspe in 1412 the Castilian Trastámara dynasty ruled.
crown-of-aragon.e: The marriage of Ferdinand II and Isabella of Castile in 1469 joined the Crown to Castile, later Habsburg Spain. The separate institutions survived until the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707-1716 that followed the War of the Spanish Succession.

catepanate-of-italy.t: Byzantine province of southern Italy governed from Bari by a catepan, the last stronghold of the Eastern Empire in Italy until the Normans took Bari in 1071.
catepanate-of-italy.o: Around 965–970 the Byzantines combined the themes of Longobardia, Calabria and Lucania under a single high-ranking governor, the catepan, based at Bari. The change answered threats from Otto I's campaigns in the south and from Arab raids.
catepanate-of-italy.r: The catepanate governed a mixed population of Latin-speaking Lombards and Greeks, with Greek monasteries flourishing in Calabria. Local revolts were frequent: Melus of Bari rebelled in 1009 and again in 1017 with Norman mercenaries, but the catepan Basil Boioannes crushed them at Cannae in 1018 and founded new towns such as Troia. The province also served as a base for George Maniakes's expedition to Sicily in 1038.
catepanate-of-italy.e: The Normans, first hired as mercenaries, conquered the province piece by piece from the 1040s. Robert Guiscard took Bari in April 1071 after a long siege, ending Byzantine rule in Italy. Greek religious and cultural influence lasted much longer in Calabria and Salento.

county-of-vermandois.t: A Picard county held by descendants of Charlemagne, whose counts were king-makers in 10th-century France before the land returned to the crown.
county-of-vermandois.o: Herbert I, a Carolingian descended from Bernard of Italy, became count of Vermandois around 896, with his seat at Saint-Quentin. His family built up lands across Picardy and Champagne during the struggles between the Carolingian kings and the Robertians.
county-of-vermandois.r: Herbert II was the most powerful lord of northern France in the 920s, holding King Charles the Simple prisoner at Péronne until the king's death in 929 and seizing the archbishopric of Reims for his young son. Later counts were less prominent. Around 1080 the heiress Adelaide married Hugh of Vermandois, brother of King Philip I and a leader of the First Crusade.
county-of-vermandois.e: In the 12th century the county passed by marriage to Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders, who lost much of it to Philip II of France in the Treaty of Boves in 1185. After the death of Countess Eleanor in 1213 the rest was absorbed by the Kingdom of France.

chios.t: Rich Ionian island state, famed for its wine and mastic, a major naval power and home of the Homeridae who claimed descent from Homer.
chios.o: Ionian Greeks settled Chios, a large island off the Erythrae peninsula, c. 1000 BCE, and it became one of the twelve members of the Ionian League. By the 7th century BCE it was a wealthy trading state with an early written law code, suggesting a council with popular elements.
chios.r: Chios exported wine and mastic and was said to be the first Greek state to buy slaves. The Homeridae guild of poets claimed descent from Homer. It sent 100 ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE. In the Delian League it kept its own fleet, before revolting in 412 BCE and later leaving the Second Athenian League in the Social War of 357 BCE.
chios.e: In 86 BCE Mithridates of the Kingdom of Pontus deported the Chians to the Black Sea; Sulla restored them and Rome confirmed their freedom. The island stayed prosperous under Roman rule and later Genoese and Ottoman masters.

canton-of-granada.t: A short-lived federalist canton proclaimed in Granada in July 1873 and ended by General Pavía's troops in August.
canton-of-granada.o: On 20 July 1873 the federalists of Granada proclaimed a sovereign canton, part of the Cantonal Rebellion that swept southern and eastern Spain against the government of the Spanish First Republic.
canton-of-granada.r: A cantonal junta took over the city, organised militias and proposed radical measures, including the demolition of some old fortifications and the taxing of the wealthy. It had little time and few resources to carry them out.
canton-of-granada.e: After crushing the cantons of Seville and Cádiz, General Manuel Pavía's forces entered Granada on 12 August 1873, and the canton dissolved without serious resistance.

county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.t: Ionian island county ruled by the Orsini and Tocco families for three centuries, a link between Italy, the Frankish Morea and Epirus.
county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.o: In 1185 the Norman admiral Margaritus of Brindisi took Cephalonia and Zakynthos from Byzantium for William II of Sicily. By about 1195 the islands were held by Matthew Orsini, of an Apulian family, who founded a hereditary lordship and placed himself in turn under the protection of the Pope, Venice and the Principality of Achaea.
county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.r: The counts ruled a Greek Orthodox population through Italian and Greek officials, with a Latin bishop alongside the Orthodox clergy. The Orsini intermarried with the rulers of the Despotate of Epirus and later acquired it. In 1357 the county passed to Leonardo I Tocco, and his son Carlo I Tocco extended Tocco power to Ioannina and Arta.
county-palatine-of-cephalonia-and-zakynt.e: Leonardo III Tocco lost his mainland lands to the Ottomans and in 1479 the islands as well, fleeing to Italy. Venice won Zakynthos in 1485 and Cephalonia in 1500, making them part of the Venetian Ionian Islands.

cyme-aeolis.t: The largest of the Aeolian cities on the Anatolian coast, home of Hesiod's father and the historian Ephorus.
cyme-aeolis.o: Aeolian Greeks founded Cyme on the coast north of the Hermus, near modern Aliağa, c. 1000 BCE. It became the leading city of the Aeolian dodecapolis, and tradition held that Hesiod's father sailed from Cyme to Boeotia. A Cymaean princess was said to have married King Midas of Phrygia.
cyme-aeolis.r: Cyme was a commercial port, minting coins from the 6th century BCE. It fell to the Kingdom of Lydia and then the Achaemenid Empire; its tyrant Aristagoras was among those guarding Darius's bridge over the Danube c. 513 BCE. The city joined the Ionian Revolt and later the Delian League, and the historian Ephorus was born there in the 4th century BCE.
cyme-aeolis.e: In the Hellenistic period Cyme passed between Seleucid and Pergamene control and kept its civic institutions. It came under Rome when the province of Asia was organised in 129 BCE, and remained a modest city into late antiquity.

cynetes.t: The people of the Algarve, named by Herodotus as the westernmost inhabitants of Europe and linked to the enigmatic south-western script.
cynetes.o: The Cynetes, or Conii, lived in the far south of modern Portugal, in the Algarve and lower Alentejo. Herodotus in the 5th century BCE called them the most westerly people of Europe, beyond the Celts. Their lands lay on the Atlantic routes that connected Tartessos with the north.
cynetes.r: Their region holds most of the inscribed stone stelae in the south-western script, the oldest writing in Iberia, dated to the 7th to 5th centuries BCE; the language they record is undeciphered and debated. Little is known of their political organisation, though Appian names a town, Conistorgis, as their chief place.
cynetes.e: In 153 BCE Lusitanians raiding Roman territory captured Conistorgis, then held by allies of Rome. The Cynetes were absorbed into the Roman province of Hispania Ulterior and later Lusitania, and their name disappears from the record.

catuvellauni.t: The leading power of late Iron Age Britain, whose king Cunobelinus ruled much of the south-east and whose sons led resistance to the Roman invasion of 43.
catuvellauni.o: The Catuvellauni held the lands north of the Thames around Hertfordshire. Cassivellaunus, who commanded British resistance to Julius Caesar in 54 BCE, is usually thought to have been their leader, with his stronghold perhaps at Wheathampstead. By the late 1st century BCE their king Tasciovanus was minting coins at Verlamion, near modern St Albans.
catuvellauni.r: Their rulers issued abundant gold coinage, some styled with the Latin REX, and imported wine, silver and fine pottery from the Roman world, as rich burials at Welwyn and Folly Lane show. Cunobelinus, ruling from about 9 to 40 CE from Camulodunum, which he took from the Trinovantes, extended influence over Kent and much of the south-east; Suetonius called him king of the Britons.
catuvellauni.e: After Cunobelinus died, his sons Togodumnus and Caratacus provoked Rome by attacking the Atrebates (Britain). Claudius invaded in 43; Togodumnus was killed and Caratacus fled west to fight on among the Silures and Ordovices until 51. The tribe became the civitas Catuvellaunorum, centred on Verulamium, in Roman Britain.

corinth.t: Wealthy trading city on the Isthmus, founder of Syracuse and Corcyra and a leading power of Archaic Greece, destroyed by Rome in 146 BCE.
corinth.o: Corinth grew in the early Iron Age on the Isthmus linking the Peloponnese to central Greece, below the fortress hill of Acrocorinth. Dorian settlers formed the city, and from the 8th century BCE it was governed by the Bacchiad clan, who founded Corcyra and Syracuse in 733 BCE.
corinth.r: Cypselus overthrew the Bacchiads c. 657 BCE, and his son Periander made Corinth a major power. Corinthian pottery dominated Mediterranean markets in the 7th century BCE, and the diolkos let ships be dragged across the Isthmus. After the tyranny an oligarchy ruled, and Corinth was a key ally in the Peloponnesian League; its quarrels with Corcyra and Athens helped start the Peloponnesian War.
corinth.e: Corinth fought Sparta in the Corinthian War of 395 to 387 BCE. Macedonian kings garrisoned Acrocorinth until Aratus took it for the Achaean League in 243 BCE. Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE; Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BCE.
corinth.re: Greek religion; cults of Poseidon and Aphrodite

commune-of-rome.t: A medieval Roman republic that revived the Senate on the Capitol in 1144 and briefly challenged the popes' rule over their own city.
commune-of-rome.o: In 1143–1144 the citizens of Rome rebelled against Pope Innocent II and his aristocratic allies, revived the Senate on the Capitoline Hill and dated their documents from the 'renewal of the Senate'. Giordano Pierleoni was named patrician.
commune-of-rome.r: The commune was governed by an elected Senate of up to 56 members, drawing on memories of ancient Rome. From 1145 the reformer Arnold of Brescia preached against papal temporal power and supported the republic. It struggled against the popes and the Papal States, and was opposed by Frederick Barbarossa, who handed Arnold over for execution in 1155. Rome also fought neighbouring towns such as Tivoli.
commune-of-rome.e: In 1188 a pact with Pope Clement III recognised the Senate in return for papal sovereignty. Around 1193 Benedetto Carushomo replaced the many senators with a single senator, and the commune's independent phase ended, though the Roman Senate continued as a city office under the popes.

caledonii.t: Confederation of the Scottish Highlands that fought Agricola at Mons Graupius and Septimius Severus, and gave its name to Caledonia.
caledonii.o: The Caledonii were a people of the central and northern Highlands, named by Ptolemy and others; Roman writers used Caledonia for northern Britain as a whole. They first appear in history when the governor Agricola marched north, and Tacitus says a host of Caledonian peoples gathered under Calgacus to meet him at Mons Graupius in 83 or 84.
caledonii.r: Romans describe them as a warrior society of clans and chiefs, without towns or coinage, living by herding and farming in a landscape of roundhouses, crannogs and brochs further north. Cassius Dio later portrays the Caledonians and Maeatae as the two main groupings beyond the walls, and tells of the Caledonian Argentocoxus, whose wife bantered with the empress Julia Domna.
caledonii.e: Defeated at Mons Graupius but never conquered, the Caledonians bought peace or raided as Roman power allowed. Septimius Severus campaigned against them from 208 to 211, and after his death Rome withdrew. By the late 3rd century Roman writers spoke instead of the Picts, whose Kingdom of the Picts absorbed the Caledonian peoples.

commonwealth-of-england.t: The republic that replaced the monarchy after the execution of Charles I in 1649, the only period without a king in English history.
commonwealth-of-england.o: After Parliament's victory in the Civil Wars, Charles I was tried and executed in January 1649. The Rump Parliament abolished the monarchy and the House of Lords and declared England a Commonwealth governed without a king. Cromwell then conquered Ireland and Scotland, which were joined to it.
commonwealth-of-england.r: Power lay with the Rump, its Council of State and the New Model Army. The regime passed the Navigation Act of 1651, fought the First Anglo-Dutch War and allowed some religious toleration while repressing Levellers and royalists. Cromwell expelled the Rump in 1653, and the nominated Barebone's Parliament failed, leading to the Protectorate.
commonwealth-of-england.e: After the Protectorate collapsed in 1659 the restored Rump briefly revived the Commonwealth. General George Monck marched from Scotland, the Convention Parliament invited Charles II back, and the monarchy was restored in May 1660 in the Kingdom of England.

county-of-barcelona.t: The leading Catalan county, whose counts united Catalonia and, through marriage with Aragon in 1137, founded the Crown of Aragon.
county-of-barcelona.o: Louis the Pious, king of Aquitaine, captured Barcelona from the Muslims in 801 after a long siege, and Charlemagne made it the main county of the Marca Hispanica. Its first count, the Goth Bera, was deposed in 820. In 878 Wilfred the Hairy received it, and after his death in 897 his heirs inherited it without royal appointment.
county-of-barcelona.r: The counts gradually gathered Girona, Osona and other counties into their hands. After Almanzor sacked Barcelona in 985, Borrell II stopped seeking Frankish protection. Ramon Berenguer I issued the first Usatges of Barcelona, the core of Catalan law, and bought rights over Carcassonne. Ramon Berenguer III gained Provence by marriage, and the city prospered through trade and tribute from the taifas.
county-of-barcelona.e: In 1137 Ramon Berenguer IV was betrothed to Petronilla, heiress of Aragon, and governed both lands. Their son Alfonso II inherited both in 1162, and the county became the core of the Crown of Aragon.

celtiberians.t: Celtic-speaking peoples of the central Iberian plateau whose long resistance to Rome ended with the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE.
celtiberians.o: The Celtiberians took shape from about the 6th century BCE in the upper Ebro, Douro and Tagus basins, in modern Soria, Guadalajara, Zaragoza and Cuenca. Ancient writers saw them as a mix of Celts and Iberians; they spoke a Celtic language and included peoples such as the Arevaci, Belli, Titti and Lusones.
celtiberians.r: They lived in fortified hill towns, or oppida, governed by councils and assemblies, with strong warrior elites, client bonds and hospitality pacts recorded on bronze tablets. They wrote Celtiberian in an adapted Iberian script, as on the Botorrita bronzes, and were famed for their swords, later adopted by the Roman army as the gladius hispaniensis.
celtiberians.e: Rome fought the Celtiberian Wars from 181 to 133 BCE, ending with Scipio Aemilianus' siege and destruction of Numantia. Many later backed Sertorius, and after his death in 72 BCE they were absorbed into Hispania Citerior and Romanised.
