county-of-la-marche.t: A border county between Poitou and the Limousin, held by the Lusignans at the height of their power and later by Armagnac and Bourbon princes.
county-of-la-marche.o: La Marche took its name from its position as a frontier zone, or march, of the duchy of Aquitaine. Around 958 Boso the Old, a lord of Charroux, held comital authority there, and his descendants ruled both La Marche and the neighbouring Périgord.
county-of-la-marche.r: A poor upland county of pasture and woodland, La Marche mattered for its strategic place between the Plantagenet and Capetian spheres. From 1199 the Lusignans held it; Hugh X married Isabella of Angoulême, widow of King John, and joined a failed revolt against Louis IX in 1242. Guéret and Charroux were its main centres.
county-of-la-marche.e: After the Lusignan line ended in 1308, Philip IV took the county. It passed to the Bourbons, the Armagnacs and back to the Bourbons as an appanage, until Francis I confiscated the lands of Constable Charles of Bourbon in 1523. It was united with the Kingdom of France in 1527.

commune-of-asti.t: A Piedmontese city-republic whose merchants and money-lenders spread across France and Flanders, giving the 'Lombard' bankers their name in the north.
commune-of-asti.o: Asti had long been ruled by its bishops, but consuls representing the citizens are recorded in 1095, making it one of the earliest communes in Piedmont. It grew rich on the trade route between Lombardy, the Alpine passes and France, and resisted both its bishop and the March of Montferrat.
commune-of-asti.r: The commune was run by consuls and later a podestà, with powerful merchant families building tower houses in the city. Asti's financiers set up pawn and loan banks across France, Savoy, the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Frederick Barbarossa burned the city in 1155, but it recovered and won a wide rural territory. The Palio of Asti horse race is first recorded in 1275.
commune-of-asti.e: Faction strife between the Solaro and de Castello families led the city to submit to outside lords, including the Angevins, and in 1342 to Luchino Visconti of the Lordship of Milan. Asti later passed as a dowry to the Orléans and then to the Duchy of Savoy.

county-of-valentinois.t: A Rhône valley county around Valence and Die held by the Poitiers family, later turned into a duchy for Cesare Borgia and Diane de Poitiers.
county-of-valentinois.o: In the early 12th century the Poitiers family, of uncertain origin, established itself as counts in the Valentinois, the lands around Valence on the left bank of the Rhône. By the 13th century they had also acquired the Diois to the east, forming the united county of Valentinois and Diois.
county-of-valentinois.r: The counts ruled a land of river trade, vineyards and Alpine valleys, holding their lands within the Kingdom of Arles. Much of their energy went into long struggles with the bishops of Valence and Die, who claimed lordship over the cities, and with the neighbouring dauphins of Viennois.
county-of-valentinois.e: The last count, Louis II of Poitiers, bequeathed the county to the Dauphin of France, and it passed to the crown in 1419 despite claims by Savoy. Louis XII later made it a duchy for Cesare Borgia in 1498, and Henry II gave it to Diane de Poitiers.

commune-of-pavia.t: The old Lombard royal capital turned city-republic, a loyal imperial ally and Milan's bitter rival until the Visconti took it in 1359.
commune-of-pavia.o: Pavia had been the capital of the Kingdom of the Lombards and the coronation city of the Kingdom of Italy (medieval). Around 1100 its citizens organised a commune under consuls, inheriting the city's royal palace traditions and a renowned school of law.
commune-of-pavia.r: Consuls and later a podestà ruled the city, which stood firmly with the emperors against Milan, fighting it repeatedly in the 12th and 13th centuries. Pavia controlled the confluence of the Ticino and the Po and much of the Lomellina. Its churches, such as San Michele Maggiore where kings were crowned and San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro with Saint Augustine's tomb, reflected its royal past. The Beccaria family dominated in the 14th century.
commune-of-pavia.e: Galeazzo II Visconti captured Pavia in 1359 after a long siege, absorbing it into the Lordship of Milan. The Visconti built a castle there, founded the university in 1361 and later the Certosa di Pavia.

commune-of-alessandria.t: A new city founded by the Lombard League in 1168 and named after Pope Alexander III, which held out against Frederick Barbarossa's siege.
commune-of-alessandria.o: The Lombard League founded Alessandria in 1168 at the confluence of the Tanaro and Bormida, settling people from nearby villages to block imperial allies such as Pavia and the March of Montferrat. The city was named in honour of Pope Alexander III.
commune-of-alessandria.r: Hastily fortified, Alessandria withstood a six-month siege by Frederick Barbarossa in 1174–1175, a key blow to the emperor before Legnano. In 1183 the city made peace with the emperor and was briefly renamed Caesarea. Governed by consuls and later a podestà, it fought its neighbours, especially the marquises of Montferrat, for control of the surrounding plain.
commune-of-alessandria.e: After periods under Montferrat and other lords, Alessandria passed in 1348 to Luchino Visconti and became part of the Lordship of Milan. It was ceded to the Duchy of Savoy in 1713.

caliphate-of-cordoba.t: The Umayyad caliphate of al-Andalus, which made Córdoba the largest city in western Europe and a centre of learning before collapsing in 1031.
caliphate-of-cordoba.o: Abd al-Rahman III, emir from 912, restored Umayyad control over the rebellious regions of al-Andalus. In 929 he proclaimed himself caliph, challenging both the Abbasids and the new Fatimid caliphate in North Africa, and took Ceuta and other ports across the Strait.
caliphate-of-cordoba.r: The caliphate was a centralised state with a professional army, a strong navy and a wealthy treasury. Abd al-Rahman III built the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra, and al-Hakam II gathered a vast library and enlarged the Great Mosque. Muslims, Christians and Jews took part in a flourishing culture of science, medicine and poetry. From 978 the hajib Almanzor ruled for the weak Hisham II and raided the Christian north, sacking Santiago in 997.
caliphate-of-cordoba.e: After Almanzor's sons died, civil war broke out in 1009, Madinat al-Zahra was sacked, and caliphs followed in quick succession. In 1031 the Córdoban notables abolished the caliphate, and al-Andalus split into the taifa kingdoms.

county-of-boulogne.t: A Channel-coast county whose counts fought at Hastings, ruled Crusader Jerusalem and married into the English throne.
county-of-boulogne.o: Boulogne took shape in the late 9th and early 10th centuries under counts linked to the house of Flanders; Adalulf, a son of Baldwin II of Flanders, held it in the 910s. The port's position on the shortest crossing to England shaped its history from the start.
county-of-boulogne.r: The counts drew wealth from the port, cross-Channel trade and lands in England. Eustace II fought for William the Conqueror at Hastings in 1066, and his sons Godfrey of Bouillon and Baldwin I led the First Crusade and ruled Jerusalem. Countess Matilda married Stephen of England. Count Renaud de Dammartin fought against Philip II at Bouvines in 1214 and lost his lands.
county-of-boulogne.e: The county passed through the houses of Auvergne and La Tour before the Burgundian State took it in 1435. After Charles the Bold's death, Louis XI seized it in 1477 and placed it under the Virgin of Boulogne, holding it directly for the Kingdom of France.

confederate-ireland.t: The Catholic government formed at Kilkenny during the Irish Confederate Wars, which ruled most of Ireland in the 1640s until Cromwell's conquest.
confederate-ireland.o: The rebellion of October 1641 by Catholic Irish gentry spread across the island. In 1642 Catholic clergy and lords formed the Confederation of Kilkenny, a government loyal to Charles I but demanding Catholic rights and self-government for Ireland.
confederate-ireland.r: A General Assembly and a Supreme Council governed, raising taxes and armies. Its motto was 'Irishmen united for God, King and country'. The papal nuncio Rinuccini divided the Confederates over peace with the king. Owen Roe O'Neill won the Battle of Benburb in 1646, while Thomas Preston led the Leinster army.
confederate-ireland.e: The Confederation dissolved itself in 1649 to ally with the royalists under Ormond. Oliver Cromwell's campaign from 1649 and the surrender of the last Irish forces in 1652 ended it, followed by massive land confiscation under the Commonwealth of England.

commune-of-novara.t: A Piedmontese city-republic between Milan and Vercelli, caught for two centuries between its larger neighbours until absorbed by the Visconti.
commune-of-novara.o: Novara, an old Roman town on the road from Milan to Turin, had a commune governed by consuls by 1116, gradually taking power from its bishops and the counts of Biandrate.
commune-of-novara.r: The commune was governed by consuls and later a podestà. It joined the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa, but its position between Milan and Vercelli made it a frequent battleground. Grain farming in its countryside and traffic on the road to the western Alps supported the town. In the 13th and 14th centuries the Tornielli and Brusati families led rival factions.
commune-of-novara.e: In 1332 Novara submitted to Azzone Visconti and became part of the Lordship of Milan. It remained Milanese until passing to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1738.

county-of-zeeland.t: The island county at the mouths of the Scheldt, Maas and Rhine, disputed by Holland and Flanders and later a stronghold of the Dutch Revolt.
county-of-zeeland.o: The islands of Zeeland had long been disputed between the counts of Flanders and the counts of Holland, who shared them in a complex arrangement. By the Treaty of Paris in 1323 Flanders gave up its claims, and Zeeland became a county ruled by the counts of Holland, with Middelburg as its main town.
county-of-zeeland.r: Zeeland was a land of reclaimed islands, dykes and seaports. Middelburg, Zierikzee, Veere and Flushing traded in wine, salt, cloth and fish, and the islands were vulnerable to great floods. The county had its own estates but shared rulers with the County of Holland, passing with it to the Wittelsbachs, the Burgundian State and the Habsburgs.
county-of-zeeland.e: In 1572 the Sea Beggars took Flushing, and Zeeland became, with Holland, the core of the Dutch Revolt. It joined the Union of Utrecht in 1579, and after the Act of Abjuration of 1581 it was a province of the Dutch Republic.

caereni.t: People of the far north-west of Scotland, named only by Ptolemy, living on the Atlantic coast of Sutherland.
caereni.o: The Caereni appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the north-western mainland of Scotland, north of the Carnonacae, usually located in western Sutherland around Assynt and Kinlochbervie. Their name has been interpreted as meaning 'sheep folk', though this is uncertain.
caereni.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions. The Atlantic coast of Sutherland was a thinly peopled land of rock, bog and sea lochs, and its inhabitants lived in roundhouses and brochs, herding livestock, fishing and farming small patches of better land.
caereni.e: The Caereni are not mentioned again. Their region later formed part of the lands of the Picts and from the 9th century came under the control of Norse settlers and the earls of Orkney.

county-of-aversa.t: The first Norman lordship in southern Italy, granted to mercenaries in 1030 and the springboard for the Norman conquest of the south.
county-of-aversa.o: In 1030 Duke Sergius IV of the Duchy of Naples rewarded the Norman mercenary leader Rainulf Drengot with the town and district of Aversa, between Naples and Capua, to guard his frontier against the Principality of Capua. Rainulf's band became a magnet for further adventurers arriving from Normandy.
county-of-aversa.r: Aversa was a military lordship in which a small warrior elite of French-speaking Normans ruled a Lombard and Italo-Romance population. Its counts sold their swords to whichever of Naples, Capua, Salerno or the Byzantines paid best, gaining recognition from Emperor Conrad II in 1038. Rainulf founded a bishopric in the town, and the county drew in Norman knights who later served in Apulia.
county-of-aversa.e: In 1058 Count Richard Drengot captured Capua and took the title of prince. Aversa was absorbed into the Principality of Capua, and its warriors had by then helped launch the conquests that created the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria.

creones.t: People of the west Highland coast of Scotland, named only in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography.
creones.o: The Creones are known solely from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the western seaboard of Scotland north of the Epidii, usually located somewhere between Lorn, Ardnamurchan and Knoydart. Their name has no clear meaning, and some editors read it as a corrupted form.
creones.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or society. The rugged coast and sea lochs of this region were settled in small communities living in duns, crannogs and roundhouses, relying on fishing, herding and limited farming. Ptolemy's information probably came from sailors who passed along the coast, perhaps during Agricola's fleet operations.
creones.e: The Creones are not mentioned again. Their region was later divided between the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata in the south and the Picts further north.

cait.t: A Pictish province in the far north of mainland Scotland, whose name survives in Caithness and in Gaelic Cataibh for Sutherland.
cait.o: Cait is one of the seven Pictish provinces named after the legendary sons of Cruithne. The name, perhaps 'cat people', survives in Caithness, the Norse 'headland of the Cats', and Gaelic Cataibh, the name for Sutherland.
cait.r: Nothing reliable is known of its government or rulers. Broch towers and later Pictish symbol stones show a long-settled farming and seafaring population in the region.
cait.e: From the 9th century Norse settlers from Orkney took over Caithness, which came under the Earldom of Orkney. The area was gradually brought into the Kingdom of Scotland in the 12th and 13th centuries.

castilian-almeria.t: The great Muslim port of Almería under Christian rule for a decade after its capture by a Castilian-led crusade in 1147.
castilian-almeria.o: In 1147 Alfonso VII of Castile, styled Emperor of Spain, led a coalition including Genoa, Pisa, Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona and García Ramírez of Navarre against Almería, then a corsair base. The city fell in October 1147, and the Genoese received a share of it.
castilian-almeria.r: Almería was held as an isolated outpost far from Castilian territory, garrisoned by Castilian troops while Genoa sought trading privileges. Much of the Muslim population had been killed, enslaved or had fled, and the economy declined. The conquest was celebrated in the Latin Poem of Almería.
castilian-almeria.e: In 1157 the Almohads besieged and recaptured the city. Alfonso VII, failing to relieve it, died on his way home. Almería remained Muslim until 1489, when it surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs.

cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.t: Breakaway Byzantine realm on Cyprus ruled by the self-proclaimed emperor Isaac Komnenos until Richard the Lionheart conquered the island in 1191.
cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.o: Isaac Komnenos, a great-nephew of Emperor Manuel I, had been governor in Cilicia and a prisoner of the Armenians. After his ransom he arrived in Cyprus in 1184 with forged imperial letters, took over the government and proclaimed himself emperor, refusing to recognise Andronikos I in Constantinople.
cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.r: Isaac ruled from Nicosia with mercenaries and was remembered by Cypriots as harsh and grasping, seizing property and abusing local nobles. He secured his position by allying with William II of Sicily, whose fleet defeated a Byzantine expedition sent by Isaac II Angelos in 1186-1187, and reportedly with Saladin. The island remained Greek Orthodox and Greek-speaking.
cyprus-under-isaac-komnenos.e: In May 1191 ships of the Third Crusade carrying Richard I's sister and his betrothed Berengaria were stranded at Limassol. Isaac's mistreatment of them gave Richard a pretext: he conquered Cyprus within weeks and held Isaac in silver chains. Richard soon sold the island to the Knights Templar.

canton-of-malaga.t: A federalist canton proclaimed in Málaga during the Cantonal Rebellion of 1873, one of the last in Andalusia to dissolve.
canton-of-malaga.o: In July 1873 the federal republicans of Málaga, a city with a strong radical movement, declared it a sovereign canton, joining the wave of cantonal risings against the central government of the Spanish First Republic.
canton-of-malaga.r: Local federalists ran the city through a cantonal committee and volunteer militias. The canton avoided open battle with the government and was torn by quarrels among its own factions over how far to break with Madrid.
canton-of-malaga.e: As the government regained control of Andalusia after General Pavía's campaign against the Canton of Seville and the Canton of Cádiz, the Málaga canton dissolved without a major fight in the late summer of 1873.

commune-of-vicenza.t: A Veneto city-republic that founded a short-lived university and spent much of its history under the rule of stronger neighbours.
commune-of-vicenza.o: Vicenza, between Verona and Padua, had consuls by 1147 after its citizens took power from the bishop. It joined the Veronese League in 1164 and then the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa.
commune-of-vicenza.r: The commune was governed by consuls and later a podestà. A university was founded in 1204 but soon faded. From the 1230s the city came under Ezzelino III da Romano, and after his fall Padua controlled Vicenza from 1266. Wool and silk were its main trades, and its noble families held castles in the surrounding hills and the Berici hills to the south. Like its neighbours, it was split by feuds between Guelph and Ghibelline families.
commune-of-vicenza.e: In 1311 Cangrande della Scala took Vicenza, and it became part of the Lordship of Verona. In 1404 it submitted to the Republic of Venice, which ruled it until 1797.

cherusci.t: The Germanic people of Arminius, whose ambush of three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE ended Rome's plan to rule Germany to the Elbe.
cherusci.o: The Cherusci lived in the region of the middle Weser and the Harz foothills. Caesar mentions them in 53 BCE as neighbours of the Suebi. After the campaigns of Drusus from 12 BCE they became Roman allies, and their noble sons, among them Arminius, served in the Roman army and received Roman citizenship.
cherusci.r: Cheruscan society was led by noble families competing for power and Roman favour; Arminius' rival Segestes stayed loyal to Rome. In 9 CE Arminius led a coalition that destroyed the legions of Publius Quinctilius Varus. He then fought Germanicus to a standstill in 15 to 16 and defeated Maroboduus in 17, before being murdered by kinsmen around 21.
cherusci.e: Internal feuding weakened the Cherusci; in 47 Rome sent Arminius' nephew Italicus to rule them. Tacitus, writing around 98, describes them as worn down and overshadowed by the Chatti. They disappear soon afterwards, probably absorbed into the peoples who later formed the Saxons.

county-of-angouleme.t: Medieval county of the Charente whose heiress Isabella married King John of England and whose lords included the Lusignans.
county-of-angouleme.o: In 866 Charles the Bald appointed his kinsman Vulgrin I count of Angoulême and Périgord to defend the region against Viking raids. His descendants, the Taillefer line, named after William II Taillefer, held Angoulême for more than three centuries.
county-of-angouleme.r: The counts were vassals of the dukes of Aquitaine and controlled the Charente valley, with Angoulême on its fortified hill. The cathedral of Saint-Pierre, rebuilt in the 12th century, shows the domed Romanesque style of the region.
county-of-angouleme.e: Isabella of Angoulême married King John of England in 1200 and later Hugh X of Lusignan, whose family then held the county. On the death of the last Lusignan heir in 1308 it passed to the French crown. It was later an appanage of the Valois-Angoulême branch, which gave France Francis I.

county-of-auvergne.t: The county of the volcanic Massif Central, centred on Clermont, where Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade in 1095.
county-of-auvergne.o: Auvergne was ruled in the late 9th century by William the Pious as part of his Aquitanian power. In the later 10th century the viscounts of Clermont took the comital title, and by around 980 they governed the county as hereditary counts under the loose overlordship of the dukes of Aquitaine.
county-of-auvergne.r: The county was a land of uplands, pasture and Romanesque churches, with the bishops of Clermont a rival power in the city. In 1095 Urban II proclaimed the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont. In the 12th century a family dispute split off the Dauphiné of Auvergne, and Philip II's campaigns from 1209 seized much of the county for the crown.
county-of-auvergne.e: The remaining county, centred on Vic-le-Comte, passed to the La Tour family and through Madeleine de la Tour d'Auvergne to her daughter Catherine de' Medici. The royal lands of Auvergne, held by the Bourbons, were confiscated after 1523 and united with the Kingdom of France in 1531.

commune-of-perugia.t: A proud Umbrian hill-city republic, nominally papal but largely independent for four centuries, until crushed in the Salt War of 1540.
commune-of-perugia.o: Perugia, an ancient Etruscan city, had consuls by 1139. Though within the lands claimed by the Papal States, it governed itself and conquered much of central Umbria, including rival Assisi and Foligno.
commune-of-perugia.r: The commune was usually Guelph and allied with the papacy, but guarded its autonomy. Elected priors ruled from the Palazzo dei Priori, and the Fontana Maggiore by Nicola and Giovanni Pisano was completed in 1278. The university was founded in 1308. In the 15th century the condottiere Braccio da Montone ruled the city, and later the Baglioni family dominated it. The painter Perugino worked there.
commune-of-perugia.e: In 1540 Perugia rebelled against a new salt tax imposed by Pope Paul III. Papal troops crushed the Salt War, and the pope built the Rocca Paolina fortress over the Baglioni houses, ending the city's autonomy.

county-palatine-of-durham.t: The palatinate where the bishops of Durham ruled as prince-bishops for more than seven centuries, guarding England's northern frontier.
county-palatine-of-durham.o: The bishops of Durham inherited the lands and prestige of the community of Saint Cuthbert, whose shrine moved to Durham in 995. William the Conqueror appointed Walcher of Lorraine bishop in 1071 and gave him the earldom of Northumbria in 1075, joining spiritual and secular power on the Scottish border.
county-palatine-of-durham.r: The bishops had their own courts, chancery, mint, sheriff and army, and royal writs did not normally run between the Tyne and the Tees. Durham Cathedral and Castle, built from 1093, expressed their power. Bishops such as Antony Bek and Thomas Langley were leading royal servants. Coal and lead mining added to their wealth.
county-palatine-of-durham.e: The Tudors curbed the palatinate's independence in 1536. The Durham (County Palatine) Act of 1836 transferred its remaining secular powers to the crown, and the University of Durham was founded with part of the bishops' endowment.

chauci.t: A Germanic seafaring people of the North Sea coast who lived on raised mounds amid the tides and later raided Roman Gaul by sea.
chauci.o: The Chauci lived along the North Sea coast between the Ems and the Elbe. They enter Roman history in 12 BCE, when Drusus led a naval expedition along their coast and made them allies. They supported Rome against Arminius, but kept their independence after Roman forces withdrew from Germany.
chauci.r: Pliny the Elder, who saw their land, describes people living on artificial mounds (terpen or Wurten) among tidal flats, fishing and burning peat for fuel. Tacitus praises them as the noblest of the Germans, preferring justice to plunder. Their coastal position made them skilled seafarers, and in 41 and 47 they raided the coast of Gaul under the leader Gannascus.
chauci.e: Chaucian sea raids continued into the late 2nd century. The name vanishes in the 3rd century, when the coastal peoples between Ems and Elbe merged with others into the Saxons, who took up the same raiding along the coasts of Gaul and Britain.

county-of-empuries.t: A Catalan coastal county in the Empordà, ruled from Castelló d'Empúries by its own counts for six centuries.
county-of-empuries.o: The county took its name from the ancient Greek city of Emporion and was created by the Franks in the early 9th century within the Marca Hispanica. From the later 9th century it was held with Roussillon by the descendants of Count Sunyer, until the two were separated in 991.
county-of-empuries.r: The counts moved their seat from Sant Martí d'Empúries to Castelló d'Empúries, where they built a large Gothic church. The county controlled the fertile Empordà plain and a coastline exposed to Viking and Saracen raids. Its counts were often in conflict with the counts of Barcelona and the bishops of Girona, while remaining vassals of the House of Barcelona.
county-of-empuries.e: After centuries of semi-independence, the county was absorbed into the royal domain of the Crown of Aragon in 1402. The title later passed to branches of the royal family and then to the Dukes of Segorbe and Medinaceli.

canton-of-unterwalden.t: One of the three founding cantons of the Swiss Confederacy, a mountain community on Lake Lucerne that was always split into two self-governing halves.
canton-of-unterwalden.o: The valleys south of Lake Lucerne, Obwalden around Sarnen and Nidwalden around Stans, were rural communities under scattered lordships, including the Habsburgs. Nidwalden swore the Federal Charter of 1291 with the Canton of Uri and the Canton of Schwyz, and Obwalden soon joined, so Unterwalden counted among the three original forest cantons of the Old Swiss Confederacy.
canton-of-unterwalden.r: Each half held its own Landsgemeinde, an open-air assembly of free men that elected officials and passed laws, and the two shared a single seat at the federal Diet. The economy rested on cattle, cheese and mercenary service abroad. Unterwalden remained firmly Catholic during the Reformation and stood with the other inner cantons against Zürich and Bern.
canton-of-unterwalden.e: When France imposed the Helvetic Republic in 1798, Nidwalden resisted and was crushed in September 1798 with heavy loss of civilian life. After 1803 the two halves re-emerged and today survive as the separate cantons of Obwalden and Nidwalden.

cenel-ngabrain.t: The dominant kindred of Dal Riata in Kintyre, whose kings, from Aedan mac Gabrain onwards, most often held the overkingship of Gaelic Argyll.
cenel-ngabrain.o: Cenel nGabrain traced its descent to Gabran, said to be a grandson of Fergus Mor, and held Kintyre, Arran and nearby lands in the 6th century. Its leading king, Aedan mac Gabrain, was ordained by Columba of Iona according to Adomnan, and campaigned widely in northern Britain before his defeat by Aethelfrith of Bernicia at Degsastan in 603.
cenel-ngabrain.r: The kindred controlled the hillfort of Dunadd for much of its history and competed with Cenel Loairn for the overkingship. Its rulers patronised Iona and fought both Picts and Britons of Alt Clut. The Senchus fer nAlban records its houses and duties to supply ships.
cenel-ngabrain.e: Defeat at Mag Rath in 637 under Domnall Brecc, and later Pictish conquest, eroded its standing. Kenneth MacAlpin, founder of the Kingdom of Scotland in the 840s, was traditionally counted among its descendants, giving the kindred a central place in Scottish royal genealogy.

county-of-pallars.t: A remote Pyrenean county in the Noguera Pallaresa valley that broke away from Frankish Toulouse and split in two in 1011.
county-of-pallars.o: Pallars, the mountain valleys of the Noguera Pallaresa in north-western Catalonia, was a district of the County of Toulouse until around 872, when Ramon I made Pallars and Ribagorza a hereditary lordship of his own.
county-of-pallars.r: The county was a land of herders and small farmers in high valleys, with castles guarding against raids from the Muslim lands to the south and monasteries such as Santa Maria de Gerri. Its counts stayed largely independent of both the Franks and Barcelona, and ruled with little written administration.
county-of-pallars.e: After Ramon I's death Ribagorza separated. In 1011 Pallars was divided between two brothers into Pallars Jussà and Pallars Sobirà. Pallars Jussà passed to the counts of Barcelona in 1192, while Pallars Sobirà survived until it was confiscated by the Crown of Aragon in 1487.

chatti.t: A disciplined Germanic people of Hesse who resisted Rome for two centuries and are often seen as ancestors of the Hessians.
chatti.o: The Chatti lived in the hill country of the upper Weser, Fulda and Eder, roughly modern northern Hesse. They appear in Roman sources around 10 BCE, when Drusus campaigned against them. Germanicus burned their chief centre, Mattium, in 15 CE, but Rome never brought them under lasting control.
chatti.r: Tacitus describes the Chatti as unusually well organised for Germans: they chose leaders, kept ranks, entrenched camps and planned campaigns. Young warriors wore an iron ring and left their hair uncut until they had killed an enemy. They farmed the fertile Hessian basins and fought regular wars with the Hermunduri over salt springs.
chatti.e: Domitian fought the Chatti in 83 to 85 and pushed the frontier forward along the Taunus and Wetterau, the line later fortified as the Limes. After about 260 they appear among the Franks. Their name is generally linked to the later Hessians, though the connection is debated.

cenomani.t: Celtic people of the plain around Brescia and Verona who, unlike other Cisalpine Gauls, were usually allies of Rome.
cenomani.o: Livy describes the Cenomani as Gauls who crossed the Alps under a leader named Elitovius in the 5th or 4th century BCE and settled in the lands around Brixia (Brescia) and Verona, between the Insubres and the Veneti.
cenomani.r: Brixia was their main centre. They farmed the plain and traded with the Veneti and Etruscans. Their relations with their Celtic neighbours were often hostile, and in 225 BCE they joined the Veneti in sending troops to help Rome against the Insubres and Boii. Apart from joining a revolt in 200–197 BCE, they remained Roman allies.
cenomani.e: After 197 BCE the Cenomani stayed loyal and were gradually Romanised. Their towns received Latin rights in 89 BCE and full citizenship in 49 BCE. Brixia became a Roman colony and Verona a leading town of northern Italy.

cispadane-republic.t: A short-lived French-backed republic south of the Po whose congress adopted the green, white and red tricolour, ancestor of the Italian flag.
cispadane-republic.o: In 1796 French victories ended Este rule in Modena and papal rule in Bologna and Ferrara. Delegates of Bologna, Ferrara, Modena and Reggio met in congress at Reggio and Modena, and in December 1796 proclaimed the Cispadane Republic.
cispadane-republic.r: On 7 January 1797 the congress at Reggio adopted the green, white and red tricolour as its flag, now celebrated as the birth of the Italian flag. The republic drafted a constitution modelled on the French Directory and held elections in early 1797. It depended entirely on French protection, and Bologna was its main centre.
cispadane-republic.e: Only months later, in July 1797, Napoleon merged the Cispadane Republic with the Transpadane Republic to create the Cisalpine Republic.

carlist-state.t: The counter-state of the Carlist pretender Carlos VII in the Basque Country and Navarre during the Third Carlist War, with its capital at Estella.
carlist-state.o: In 1872, as the Sexenio Democrático unsettled Spain, the traditionalist pretender Carlos VII, Duke of Madrid, launched the Third Carlist War under the banner of God, Fatherland and King. His forces took control of much of rural Navarre, the Basque provinces and parts of Catalonia.
carlist-state.r: The Carlists organised a real administration from Estella: ministries, courts, a postal service with its own stamps, coinage and a university at Oñati. They restored the Basque and Navarrese fueros and enforced strict Catholicism. Their armies besieged Bilbao in 1874 but never took a major city.
carlist-state.e: After the Bourbon restoration in Restoration Spain, government armies advanced. Estella fell in February 1876, and Carlos VII crossed into France. The Basque fueros were then largely abolished, though Carlism survived as a political movement.

callaeci.t: The hillfort peoples of north-western Iberia, whose castro culture shaped Galicia and northern Portugal and who held out against Rome until 19 BCE.
callaeci.o: The Callaeci, or Gallaeci, occupied the north-west of Iberia north of the Douro, in modern Galicia and northern Portugal. Their culture grew from the Late Bronze Age into the Iron Age castro culture, marked by hundreds of fortified hilltop settlements of round stone houses.
callaeci.r: They were divided into many small communities rather than one state, each based on a castro such as Citânia de Briteiros or Santa Tecla. They mined gold and tin, worked bronze and gold into torcs, and built sauna-like bathhouses with carved stones. They spoke a Celtic language, worshipped gods such as Bandua, and erected stone warrior statues.
callaeci.e: Decimus Junius Brutus campaigned among them in 137 BCE and took the name Callaicus, but conquest was completed only in Augustus' Cantabrian Wars, ending in 19 BCE. Their land became the Roman region and later province of Gallaecia.

commune-of-verona.t: A city-republic on the Adige that led resistance to Frederick Barbarossa and then fell under the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano.
commune-of-verona.o: Verona, guarding the route from the Brenner Pass into Italy, had consuls by 1136. It led the Veronese League of 1164 against Frederick Barbarossa's officials and then joined the wider Lombard League.
commune-of-verona.r: Consuls and later a podestà governed the city, whose wealth came from the Adige trade and the road to Germany. The Romanesque basilica of San Zeno was rebuilt in the 12th century. From the 1220s the city was dominated by Ezzelino III da Romano, a Ghibelline ally of Frederick II whose harsh rule over Verona, Vicenza and Padua made him a byword for tyranny.
commune-of-verona.e: After Ezzelino's death in 1259 the city chose Mastino I della Scala as its leader, and by 1262 communal government had given way to the Lordship of Verona of the Scaliger family.

condrusi.t: One of the Germani Cisrhenani of the Belgian uplands, remembered in the name of the Condroz.
condrusi.o: Caesar names the Condrusi with the Eburones, Caeroesi and Paemani as Germani living west of the Rhine, and calls them clients of the Treveri. They lived south of the Meuse in the region still called the Condroz, between Namur and Liège.
condrusi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or settlements.
condrusi.e: They joined the Belgic league in 57 BCE. In 53 BCE they asked Caesar to spare them from his war on the Eburones. Under Rome they were absorbed into the civitas of the Tungri.

county-of-anjou.t: The Loire Valley county whose aggressive counts built the power base of the Plantagenets and later passed to a line of French royal princes.
county-of-anjou.o: Anjou emerged in the late 9th century, when the Frankish crown entrusted the region around Angers to local magnates facing Breton and Viking raids. Ingelger held authority there, and his son Fulk the Red was styled count by about 930, founding a dynasty that turned a frontier command into a hereditary principality.
county-of-anjou.r: The counts ruled from Angers with a dense network of stone castles, many built by Fulk Nerra (987–1040), which let them push into Touraine and Maine. Anjou was a wine and river-trade region with powerful abbeys. Geoffrey Plantagenet conquered Normandy in the 1140s, and his son Henry II joined Anjou to England and Aquitaine in the Angevin Empire.
county-of-anjou.e: Philip II of France seized Anjou in 1204. It was granted as an appanage to Charles of Anjou in 1246, became a duchy in 1360 for Louis I, and its last great duke, René of Anjou, died in 1480. Louis XI then annexed it to the Kingdom of France.

carpi.t: Free Dacian people east of the Carpathians who raided Roman Dacia and Moesia throughout the 3rd century until Rome resettled them inside the empire.
carpi.o: The Carpi lived in Moldavia, east of the Carpathians and outside Roman Dacia, from the 2nd century CE. They are usually identified with the Poienești archaeological culture of farming villages and cremation cemeteries, and are considered a Dacian people.
carpi.r: They lived in unfortified villages under tribal leaders, farming and herding. In the crisis of the 3rd century they joined the Goths in raids across the Danube, besieging Marcianopolis and attacking Dacia. The emperor Philip the Arab defeated them in 247, and several emperors took the victory title Carpicus.
carpi.e: Aurelian, and then Diocletian and Galerius around 295–305, defeated them and moved large numbers into Pannonia and Moesia. The last mention comes under Constantine around 318, after which the remaining Carpi merged into the Gothic and Roman worlds.

county-of-lantaron.t: A small frontier county of the Kingdom of Asturias and León in the Ebro gorges, between Castile and Álava.
county-of-lantaron.o: Lantarón, near the Ebro gorges on the borders of Álava and Burgos, became a county at the end of the 9th century, when Count Gonzalo Téllez is recorded as ruling Lantarón and Cerezo. It was one of several frontier counties defending the eastern flank of the Kingdom of Asturias.
county-of-lantaron.r: The counts were military governors for the kings of Asturias and León, holding castles such as Cerezo against raids from the Banu Qasi and Córdoba. The population of the area was a mix of Basque and Romance speakers living in small villages.
county-of-lantaron.e: In the 930s the county was absorbed by Fernán González into the growing County of Castile, and Lantarón ceased to be a separate county.

county-of-alava.t: A Basque frontier county of the Kingdom of Asturias, defending the upper Ebro against the Banu Qasi before merging with Castile.
county-of-alava.o: Álava appears in the 9th-century Asturian chronicles as an eastern frontier district of the Kingdom of Asturias, facing Muslim raids up the Ebro. Counts are recorded from the 860s, among them Vela Jiménez, who held the castle of Cellorigo against Córdoba in 882 and 883.
county-of-alava.r: Its society was largely Basque-speaking and rural, organised in valleys and villages, with the counts acting as military governors for the kings of Asturias and León. The 1025 Reja de San Millán, a list of Álava villages paying iron to the monastery of San Millán, shows a dense pattern of settlements.
county-of-alava.e: Fernán González brought Álava under his control in the 930s, linking it to the County of Castile. In the 11th century it passed between Castile and Navarre, before being integrated permanently into Castile in 1200.

commune-of-como.t: A lakeside city-republic that Milan destroyed in 1127 and Frederick Barbarossa rebuilt, home of the master builders known as the Comacine masters.
commune-of-como.o: Como, at the southern tip of Lake Como on the route to the Alpine passes, had consuls by 1109. Its quarrel with Milan over the bishopric and lake trade led to the Ten Years' War of 1118–1127, which ended with Como's destruction.
commune-of-como.r: Como was ruled by consuls and later a podestà. Allied with Frederick Barbarossa, it was rebuilt with imperial support in 1159 and remained largely Ghibelline. Its builders and stonemasons, the magistri comacini, worked across northern Italy, and the city controlled lake shipping and Alpine traffic. In the 13th and 14th centuries the Ghibelline Rusca and Guelph Vittani families fought for control.
commune-of-como.e: In 1335 Franchino Rusca surrendered the city to Azzone Visconti, and Como became part of the Lordship of Milan, later the Duchy of Milan.

caristii.t: A small people of Bizkaia and Álava between the Deba and Nervión rivers, whose Roman town Veleia lay on the road to Gaul.
caristii.o: The Caristii lived in the later Iron Age between the Deba and Nervión rivers, in modern Bizkaia and northern Álava, flanked by the Autrigones and Varduli. Their language is unknown.
caristii.r: Their society of hillfort communities is little documented. Ptolemy names their towns as Suessatium, Tullonium and Veleia, the last of which grew into the Roman town of Iruña-Veleia.
caristii.e: They came under Roman control as the conquest of the north was completed in 19 BCE and were absorbed into Hispania Tarraconensis.

county-of-loon.t: A Limburg county around Borgloon and Hasselt that remained independent for three centuries before being absorbed by the prince-bishops of Liège.
county-of-loon.o: Counts of Loon appear around 1015, when Giselbert held lands around Borgloon in the Hesbaye. They expanded north into the Kempen heathlands, and the county became one of the middle-ranking principalities of Lower Lorraine.
county-of-loon.r: Loon was largely rural, with small towns such as Hasselt and Borgloon. From the late 12th century the counts were vassals of the prince-bishops of Liège. The poet Henric van Veldeke, a founder of literature in Dutch and German, came from the county and wrote for its court circles.
county-of-loon.e: After Count Louis IV died childless in 1336, his inheritance was disputed between his heirs and the bishops of Liège. In 1366 the Prince-Bishopric of Liège annexed the county, and it remained part of the principality until 1795; it corresponds roughly to Belgian Limburg.

cornovii.t: Iron Age people of the West Midlands and Welsh borders, centred on the Wrekin, whose Roman town of Viroconium became one of the largest in Britain.
cornovii.o: The Cornovii occupied Shropshire, Cheshire and parts of Staffordshire and the Welsh borderland in the late Iron Age. Their landscape was dominated by hillforts such as the Wrekin, Titterstone Clee and the Breiddin, many of which had been occupied for centuries before the Roman period.
cornovii.r: They issued no coins and used very little pottery, so their society is known mainly from hillforts and farmsteads. Livestock farming was central, and the brine springs of Cheshire supplied salt that was traded in distinctive clay containers. No rulers are named in any source, suggesting power was held by local chiefs.
cornovii.e: The Roman army advanced into the region in the 50s, and around 55 to 60 a legionary fortress was built at Wroxeter below the Wrekin, which seems to have been abandoned. When the army left, the site became Viroconium Cornoviorum, capital of their civitas in Roman Britain and later the seat of post-Roman rulers in what became the Kingdom of Powys.

county-of-perche.t: A hilly county between Normandy and Maine whose crusading counts fought in Spain and the Holy Land before it lapsed to the French crown.
county-of-perche.o: The lords of Mortagne and Nogent gathered the forested hill country of the Perche in the 11th century, and around 1079 Geoffrey II was styled count of Perche. The county lay on the frontier between Normandy, Maine and the royal domain, and its counts balanced between the Anglo-Norman kings and the Capetians.
county-of-perche.r: Perche was a land of forests, iron and horse breeding, later famous for the Percheron. Count Rotrou III fought in the First Crusade and in Aragon's wars against the Almoravids, and married a daughter of Henry I of England. Count Thomas was killed fighting for the French prince Louis at Lincoln in 1217.
county-of-perche.e: The last count, William, bishop of Châlons, died in 1226, and Louis VIII and Louis IX absorbed the county into the royal domain of the Kingdom of France. It was later granted as an appanage to royal princes.

county-of-holland.t: The coastal county that grew from Frisian marshland into the richest province of the Low Countries and the core of the later Dutch Republic.
county-of-holland.o: The dynasty began with Gerulf, a Frisian lord granted lands by the Carolingians in the 880s, and Dirk I, who received the land around Egmond in 922. The counts were first known as counts of West Frisia, and the name Holland ('wood land') came into use around 1100.
county-of-holland.r: The counts drained peat bogs, built dykes and founded towns such as Haarlem, Delft, Leiden and Dordrecht. Dirk III defeated an imperial army at Vlaardingen in 1018; William II was elected King of the Romans in 1247 and began the Binnenhof at The Hague. Under Floris V the towns, fishing and cloth trade grew rapidly, and water boards became a hallmark of local government.
county-of-holland.e: Holland passed to the Avesnes counts of Hainaut in 1299, the Wittelsbachs in 1345 and the Burgundian State in 1433, amid the Hook and Cod wars. Under the Habsburg Netherlands it led the revolt against Spain, and after the Act of Abjuration of 1581 it became the dominant province of the Dutch Republic.

commune-of-volterra.t: An ancient Etruscan hill-city republic whose alum mines provoked a brutal Florentine sack in 1472.
commune-of-volterra.o: Volterra, one of the old Etruscan cities, was long ruled by its bishops. In the late 12th century its citizens organised a commune, and from 1208 they built the Palazzo dei Priori, the oldest surviving town hall in Tuscany.
commune-of-volterra.r: The commune was governed by consuls, then a podestà and priors, and wrestled with its bishops for control of the salt pans and mines of its territory. Alabaster carving was an ancient craft. In the 14th century the Belforti family dominated. From 1361 the city was under Florentine protection but kept its own government.
commune-of-volterra.e: A dispute over alum mines led Volterra to rebel in 1472. Federico da Montefeltro, hired by Florence under Lorenzo de' Medici, besieged and sacked the city, which was then fully absorbed into the Republic of Florence.

county-of-aragon.t: The small Pyrenean county around Jaca that gave its name to the Kingdom and later the Crown of Aragon.
county-of-aragon.o: The county arose in the early 9th century in the upper valley of the river Aragón, around Jaca, as a Frankish-backed frontier lordship. Its first known count, Aznar Galíndez I, ruled in the 800s under Carolingian protection before being expelled by rivals allied with Pamplona.
county-of-aragon.r: Aragon was a mountain county of herders and small farmers, protected by castles and monasteries such as San Juan de la Peña and San Pedro de Siresa. Its native counts of the Galindo family kept close ties with Pamplona, and in the early 10th century the heiress Andregoto Galíndez married García Sánchez I of Pamplona, bringing the county under the Navarrese crown.
county-of-aragon.e: Aragon was ruled from Pamplona until Sancho III died in 1035 and left it to his son Ramiro I, who governed it as a separate realm, the beginning of the Kingdom of Aragon, which later grew into the Crown of Aragon.

ceutrones.t: Alpine people of the Tarentaise who guarded the Little St Bernard pass and harassed Caesar's army in 58 BCE.
ceutrones.o: The Ceutrones held the upper Isère valley, the Tarentaise in Savoy, below the Little St Bernard pass. Caesar records that they and other mountain peoples attacked his legions as they crossed the Alps in 58 BCE.
ceutrones.r: Their power rested on control of the pass, one of the main routes between Gaul and northern Italy, and on herding and trade with the Salassi of the Aosta valley.
ceutrones.e: They were subdued in the Alpine campaigns of Augustus around 15 BCE and listed on the Tropaeum Alpium. Their town Axima (Aime) became Forum Claudii Ceutronum, capital of the small province of Alpes Graiae.

colophon.t: Ionian city famed for its cavalry and wealth, home of the poets Mimnermus and Xenophanes and keeper of the oracle of Apollo at Claros.
colophon.o: Colophon lay inland north-west of Ephesus and was founded by Ionian settlers c. 1000 BCE. It was one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League and in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE grew rich and powerful, its exiles seizing Smyrna from the Aeolians.
colophon.r: Colophon had a strong landed aristocracy whose cavalry was proverbial. The elegiac poet Mimnermus and the philosopher Xenophanes were Colophonians. The oracle of Apollo at Claros lay in its territory. Gyges of the Kingdom of Lydia captured its lower town in the 7th century BCE, and it then passed to the Achaemenid Empire and the Delian League.
colophon.e: Lysimachus forced many Colophonians to move to Ephesus c. 294 BCE. The city recovered, partly through its port of Notion, called New Colophon, and passed to Rome in 133 BCE, while Claros remained a major oracle into Roman times.
colophon.re: Greek religion; oracle of Apollo at Claros

commune-of-ferrara.t: A Po delta city-republic whose factional wars ended with the Este family as perpetual lords, the start of one of Italy's great dynasties.
commune-of-ferrara.o: Ferrara was held by Matilda of Canossa, who besieged it in 1101 to put down a revolt. In the years that followed, citizens formed a commune under consuls, profiting from Po river traffic and salt. The cathedral was begun in 1135.
commune-of-ferrara.r: Consuls and later a podestà ruled, but power was really contested between noble factions: the Adelardi, the Ghibelline Torelli led by Salinguerra II Torelli, and the Guelph Este marquises. Ferrara's position on the Po made it a hub for trade between Venice and the Lombard plain. Azzo VII d'Este expelled Salinguerra in 1240 with Venetian and papal help.
commune-of-ferrara.e: After Azzo VII's death in 1264, the citizens proclaimed his grandson Obizzo II d'Este perpetual lord, and the commune gave way to the Duchy of Ferrara under the Este.

county-of-zutphen.t: A short-lived county on the IJssel that merged with Guelders in the 12th century and gave its name to one of the duchy's four quarters.
county-of-zutphen.o: The county of Zutphen took shape in the mid-11th century around the trading town on the IJssel. Its early counts held lands granted by the German kings and the bishops of Utrecht, but details of its first rulers are scarce.
county-of-zutphen.r: Zutphen was a river-trade centre on the route between the Rhine and the Zuiderzee, and the county included rich farmland in the Achterhoek. Its counts were linked by marriage to the leading families of the region.
county-of-zutphen.e: Around 1138 the heiress Ermgard of Zutphen's marriage to Gerard of Wassenberg, count of Guelders, united Zutphen with the County of Guelders. It became one of the four quarters of the later Duchy of Guelders, and the town of Zutphen joined the Hanseatic League.

catalauni.t: Gallic people of Champagne around Châlons, whose plains gave their name to the battle against Attila in 451.
catalauni.o: The Catalauni are not named by Caesar and were probably part of the Remi in his time. They are known from later Roman sources as a separate community centred on Durocatalaunum (Châlons-en-Champagne) on the Marne.
catalauni.r: Nothing is known of their pre-Roman rulers. Their chalk plains were rich farmland on the route between Reims and Langres.
catalauni.e: Durocatalaunum became a separate civitas in the late Roman period and a bishopric. The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451, where Aetius and the Visigoths halted the Hunnic Empire under Attila, is named after their land.

county-of-saldana.t: The lordship of the Banu Gómez family on the upper Carrión, powerful nobles of León who sometimes allied with Almanzor.
county-of-saldana.o: In the late 9th and early 10th centuries the Leonese kings granted the lands of Saldaña, Carrión and Liébana on the upper Carrión river to Count Diego Muñoz, founder of the family later called the Banu Gómez in Arabic sources. The county was part of the resettlement of the Douro plain.
county-of-saldana.r: The counts were among the most powerful nobles of the Kingdom of León, ruling large estates and castles and often rebelling against the crown. Count García Gómez allied with Almanzor and took part in his campaigns in the 990s. The county's towns, Saldaña and Carrión, lay on the route that became the Way of St James.
county-of-saldana.e: After the decline of the Banu Gómez in the early 11th century, the county passed into the domains of the kings of León and Castile. Carrión later belonged to the Ansúrez family, and its counts appear in the legend of El Cid.

commune-of-piacenza.t: A Po crossing city-republic whose merchants and bankers traded across Europe and whose Gothic town hall still dominates its main square.
commune-of-piacenza.o: Piacenza, an old Roman colony where the Via Emilia meets the Po, had consuls by 1126. Its citizens took over the bishop's powers and controlled the river crossings and the road to Genoa.
commune-of-piacenza.r: Governed by consuls and later a podestà, Piacenza joined the Lombard League, and the preliminary talks for the Peace of Constance were held there in 1183. Its merchants and money-changers were active at the Champagne fairs and in papal finance. The Palazzo Gotico, the town hall, was begun in 1281. Ghibelline lords such as Uberto Pallavicino and later Alberto Scotti held power in the 13th century.
commune-of-piacenza.e: Rival families repeatedly invited outside lords, and in 1336 Azzone Visconti took the city into the Lordship of Milan. Piacenza later became part of the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza.

cretan-koinon.t: Loose federation of the quarrelsome Cretan city-states, active in the Hellenistic period until the Roman conquest of the island in 69-67 BCE.
cretan-koinon.o: Crete was divided among dozens of independent cities, chief among them Knossos and Gortyn, constantly at war. A common body of Cretans (koinon) appears in the 3rd century BCE, and around 216 BCE Philip V of Macedon was recognised as its protector (prostates), seeking influence over the island and its mercenaries.
cretan-koinon.r: The koinon had a council and a common court (koinodikion) to settle disputes between cities, and issued joint decrees and treaties. It never overrode local sovereignty, and wars such as the Lyttian War of the 220s BCE continued. Cretan archers served as mercenaries across the Mediterranean, and Cretan ports harboured pirates.
cretan-koinon.e: The league was revived and dissolved several times. Rome's war on piracy brought Marcus Antonius' failed attack in 71 BCE and then Quintus Caecilius Metellus' conquest of the island in 69-67 BCE, after which Crete became a Roman province with Gortyn as its capital.

county-of-foix.t: A Pyrenean county that sheltered Cathars, produced the hunter-prince Gaston Fébus and passed through Navarre to Henry IV.
county-of-foix.o: Around 1012 the lands of the count of Carcassonne were divided, and his son Bernard-Roger received the region around Foix, which became a separate county under the castle above the Ariège. His son Roger I is the first to be called count of Foix.
county-of-foix.r: The counts ruled a mountainous land of pasture and iron mines. Count Raymond-Roger fought the crusaders in the Albigensian Crusade, and many of his family supported the Cathars. In 1290 the counts inherited Béarn, and Gaston III Fébus ruled both from Orthez as a near-sovereign prince and wrote a famous hunting book.
county-of-foix.e: The house of Foix inherited the throne of Navarre in 1479, then passed to the Albrets. Through Jeanne d'Albret it reached Henry IV, who in 1607 united his personal lands, including Foix, with the Kingdom of France.

county-of-salona.t: Frankish lordship around Amfissa and Delphi in central Greece that passed from French to Catalan to Byzantine hands before falling to the Ottomans.
county-of-salona.o: Boniface of Montferrat granted Salona, the medieval name of Amfissa, to the French knight Thomas d'Autremencourt in 1205. Its castle, built on the ancient acropolis, controlled the land between Mount Parnassus and the Gulf of Corinth, including the old sanctuary of Delphi and the port of Galaxidi.
county-of-salona.r: The lords of Salona were vassals of the Principality of Achaea and neighbours of the Duchy of Athens, ruling a Greek peasant population through a small Frankish elite. Thomas III d'Autremencourt was killed in 1311 fighting the Catalan Company at the Battle of Halmyros. The Catalans took over, and the county later passed to the Fadrique family, a branch of the royal house of Sicily.
county-of-salona.e: In 1394 the widow of Louis Fadrique, Helena Kantakouzene, lost Salona to Sultan Bayezid I. It was briefly held by the Despotate of the Morea and the Knights Hospitaller in the early 15th century before the Ottomans took it permanently in 1410.

county-of-namur.t: A compact county at the meeting of the Sambre and Meuse, built around a rock fortress that later became one of the most fought-over strongholds in Europe.
county-of-namur.o: Namur emerged in the 10th century from the old district of Lomme, when local counts built their power around the castle on the rock above the Sambre and Meuse confluence. Albert I, ruling around 981, is often treated as the first well-documented count, and his family held the county for two centuries.
county-of-namur.r: Namur was a small Walloon county of river trade, forests and ironworks, an imperial fief squeezed between Liège, Hainaut, Brabant and Luxembourg. Count Henry the Blind also held Luxembourg in the 12th century. From 1263 the Dampierre counts of Flanders ruled it, and Namur's citadel grew into a major fortress.
county-of-namur.e: The bankrupt John III sold Namur to Philip the Good in 1421, and it joined the Burgundian State, then the Habsburg Netherlands. Louis XIV took the citadel in 1692 and William III retook it in 1695. France annexed the county in 1795; it is now a Belgian province.

clusium.t: Inland Etruscan city whose king Lars Porsenna, in Roman tradition, besieged Rome after the expulsion of the Tarquins.
clusium.o: Clusium, Etruscan Clevsin, modern Chiusi, overlooked the Val di Chiana, a fertile corridor linking central Etruria with the Tiber valley. It developed from Villanovan settlements and flourished from the 7th century BCE, when its distinctive canopic urns, cinerary jars with human-headed lids, show a local elite of growing wealth.
clusium.r: Clusium's power rested on agriculture in the Chiana valley and on control of routes towards the interior. Its workshops produced cinerary urns, sculptures in local stone and fine bucchero pottery, while painted tombs such as the Tomb of the Monkey show banquets and games. Roman tradition records its king Lars Porsenna, who attacked Rome around 508 BCE and possibly took it.
clusium.e: In 391 BCE Gauls attacked Clusium, an event Roman writers linked to the Gallic sack of Rome. The city came under Roman control after the wars of the early 3rd century, traditionally around the battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE, and remained a modest Roman town; Etruscan burials continued there into the 1st century BCE.

county-of-artois.t: A northern French county of cloth towns and tapestries, created as a royal appanage and later held by Burgundy and Spain before returning to France.
county-of-artois.o: Artois came to the French crown in 1191 through Isabella of Hainaut's dowry. In 1237 Louis IX created it as a county for his brother Robert I, who was killed at Mansourah in 1250 on crusade. Robert's descendants ruled it from Arras.
county-of-artois.r: Arras was a major cloth and banking town, and its tapestries became so famous that 'arras' meant a wall hanging in English and Italian. Count Robert II was killed at Courtrai in 1302, and his daughter Mahaut defended her inheritance against her nephew Robert III. In 1384 Artois passed with Flanders to Philip the Bold, joining the Burgundian State.
county-of-artois.e: After 1477 Artois stayed with the Habsburgs in the Habsburg Netherlands and Spanish Netherlands. Louis XIII took Arras in 1640, and the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 gave most of the county to the Kingdom of France.

clanricarde.t: The Gaelicised Burke lordship of south Galway, ruled by the Mac William Uachtar, which became an earldom under Henry VIII in 1543.
clanricarde.o: When William Donn de Burgh, Earl of Ulster, was murdered in 1333, his Connacht lands were seized by his kinsmen. The southern branch, led by Ulick de Burgh, adopted the Gaelic title Mac William Uachtar, the Upper Mac William, and ruled south Galway from Loughrea.
clanricarde.r: The Clanricarde Burkes adopted Irish law, language and customs, intermarrying with Gaelic families while competing with the O'Briens and with Galway town. Their battles included Knockdoe in 1504, where Ulick Fionn Burke was defeated by the Earl of Kildare. Tower houses dotted their lands.
clanricarde.e: In 1543 Ulick na gCeann Burke submitted to Henry VIII and became Earl of Clanricarde in the Kingdom of Ireland. Later earls were loyal to the crown, and Ulick Burke was made Marquess of Clanricarde in 1646.

commune-of-padua.t: A Venetian-plain city-republic that founded Italy's second university in 1222 and saw Giotto paint the Scrovegni Chapel.
commune-of-padua.o: Padua, a large Roman town that had recovered slowly from the early Middle Ages, had consuls by 1138. The commune took power from its bishop and expanded across the plain between the Brenta and the Adige.
commune-of-padua.r: Governed by consuls and later a podestà, Padua joined the Lombard League. In 1222 masters and students from Bologna founded its university. From 1237 to 1256 the city suffered under Ezzelino III da Romano. Afterwards the commune flourished: the basilica of Saint Anthony was built, Giotto painted the Scrovegni Chapel around 1305, and the scholar Albertino Mussato revived classical Latin drama. Padua ruled Vicenza for a time.
commune-of-padua.e: Pressure from Cangrande della Scala of Verona led the citizens in 1318 to make Jacopo I da Carrara their lord, beginning the Lordship of Padua.

county-of-cerdanya.t: A Pyrenean county of the Catalan heartland whose counts founded Sant Martí del Canigó before it passed to Barcelona in 1117.
county-of-cerdanya.o: The high valley of Cerdanya came under Frankish rule around 798 and was organised as a county of the Marca Hispanica, often held with neighbouring Urgell. Sunifred, father of Wilfred the Hairy, held it in the 830s and 840s, and Wilfred himself became count in 870.
county-of-cerdanya.r: From 897 Cerdanya had its own line of counts descended from Wilfred, controlling the valley, Conflent, Berga and Ripoll. The counts were great patrons of the church: Wifred II founded the monastery of Sant Martí del Canigó around 1009, and his brother Oliba became abbot of Ripoll and bishop of Vic. The county lived from mountain herding and Pyrenean trade routes.
county-of-cerdanya.e: When Count Bernat Guillem died without heirs in 1117, Cerdanya passed to Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona. It became part of the Crown of Aragon, and in 1659 the Treaty of the Pyrenees split the valley between Spain and France.

commune-of-pistoia.t: A Tuscan city-republic with some of Italy's oldest communal statutes, where the feud of Black and White Guelphs began before spreading to Florence.
commune-of-pistoia.o: Pistoia, at the foot of the Apennines between Florence and Lucca, had consuls by 1105. Its early statutes, from the 12th century, are among the oldest surviving communal law codes in Italy.
commune-of-pistoia.r: The commune was governed by consuls, then a podestà and a captain of the people. Pistoia was known for banking and metalwork and for the silver altar of Saint James in its cathedral. Around 1300 a feud within the Cancellieri family split the Guelphs into Blacks and Whites, a quarrel exported to Florence that led to Dante's exile. Florence and Lucca besieged and took Pistoia in 1305–1306.
commune-of-pistoia.e: Castruccio Castracani of Lucca seized the city in 1325. Florence later imposed a protectorate and gradually tightened control, formally annexing Pistoia in 1401, after which it remained part of the Republic of Florence.

cretan-state.t: Autonomous Crete under great-power protection from 1898, a stepping stone to union with Greece and the launch pad of Eleftherios Venizelos.
cretan-state.o: Crete rose repeatedly against Ottoman rule in the 19th century. After the revolt of 1897 and the Greco-Turkish War, Britain, France, Russia and Italy occupied the island and forced the Ottomans to accept its autonomy under nominal suzerainty. Prince George of Greece became High Commissioner in December 1898, with Chania as capital.
cretan-state.r: The Cretan State had its own constitution, assembly, gendarmerie, currency and stamps, though foreign troops remained. Prince George's autocratic style clashed with Eleftherios Venizelos, who led the Therisos revolt in 1905. Alexandros Zaimis replaced the prince in 1906. Most of the population was Greek Orthodox, with a significant Muslim minority.
cretan-state.e: In 1908 the Cretan assembly declared union with Greece. After the Balkan Wars, the Ottomans renounced Crete, and it was formally united with the Kingdom of Greece in December 1913. Venizelos had by then become prime minister of Greece.

cisalpine-republic.t: Napoleon's largest Italian sister republic, uniting Lombardy, Emilia and Romagna, and an early laboratory for a modern Italian state.
cisalpine-republic.o: On 29 June 1797 Napoleon proclaimed the Cisalpine Republic, merging the Transpadane Republic with territories that soon included the Cispadane Republic, Romagna, the Valtellina and the former Venetian cities of Bergamo, Brescia and Crema. The Treaty of Campo Formio confirmed it in October 1797.
cisalpine-republic.r: The republic had a constitution modelled on the French Directory, with Milan as capital. It reorganised its territory into departments, sold church lands and built a national guard, but the French made and unmade its governments and drew heavy contributions. Debate about Italian identity flourished in Milan.
cisalpine-republic.e: An Austro-Russian offensive overthrew the republic in 1799. Restored after Napoleon's victory at Marengo in 1800, it was transformed at the Consulta of Lyon in January 1802 into the Italian Republic (1802–1805).

canton-of-seville.t: A short-lived revolutionary canton proclaimed in Seville during the federalist Cantonal Rebellion of 1873.
canton-of-seville.o: In July 1873, impatient with the slow progress of federalism under the Spanish First Republic, radical federalists across southern and eastern Spain declared their cities sovereign cantons. Seville's federalists proclaimed their canton on 19 July 1873.
canton-of-seville.r: The cantonal junta took control of the city, raised volunteer militias and announced radical measures, including the seizure of church property and workers' reforms, intending to form part of a future federal Spain built from the bottom up.
canton-of-seville.e: Government troops under General Manuel Pavía attacked the city and, after street fighting, crushed the canton at the end of July 1873. Pavía went on to subdue the Canton of Cádiz.

county-of-castile.t: The frontier county of the Kingdom of León, made autonomous by Fernán González, that grew into the Kingdom of Castile.
county-of-castile.o: Castile, 'land of castles', began in the 9th century as a frontier district of the Kingdom of Asturias in the upper Ebro and Burgos region. Its first known count, Rodrigo, governed from around 850, and his son Diego Rodríguez Porcelos founded Burgos in 884. Several local counts governed until the territory was united.
county-of-castile.r: Count Fernán González, from about 931 to 970, gathered the Castilian counties and made his office hereditary, largely independent of León. Castile was a society of free peasant-soldiers and frontier towns, with its own customary law and a Romance dialect that became Castilian. Sancho García granted fueros to frontier settlers, and the counts fought Almanzor and his successors.
county-of-castile.e: The murder of the young Count García Sánchez in 1029 brought Castile under Sancho III of Navarre, whose son Ferdinand I ruled it and became king of León in 1037. From 1065 Castile was a kingdom in its own right under Sancho II.

county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.t: Small Westphalian county in the Rothaar hills, known as a refuge for radical Pietists and as home of the Berleburg Bible.
county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.o: The County of Sayn-Wittgenstein was divided in 1605 among the sons of Count Ludwig I. Georg received Berleburg in the northern Wittgenstein land, founding a line that would persist alongside Sayn-Wittgenstein-Hohenstein.
county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.r: The county was poor, forested upland with some iron working, governed from Berleburg Castle. Under Count Casimir in the early 18th century it became a haven for religious dissenters and radical Pietists, and the eight-volume Berleburg Bible, a mystical commentary, was published there from 1726. The counts were raised to princely rank in 1792.
county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.e: The territory was mediatised in 1806 and placed under the Grand Duchy of Hesse, then passed to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1816 as part of the Province of Westphalia. The princes of Sayn-Wittgenstein-Berleburg still live at Berleburg Castle.

county-of-evreux.t: A Norman county that became the appanage of a royal branch whose members, as kings of Navarre, schemed against the Valois.
county-of-evreux.o: Around 989 Duke Richard I of Normandy created the county of Évreux for his son Robert, archbishop of Rouen. Robert's descendants held it as major Norman barons, and it later passed to the Montfort family, frequently caught up in the wars between Normandy and France.
county-of-evreux.r: Évreux was a rich farming district on the road from Paris to Rouen, with a cathedral city as its centre. Philip II obtained it from John of England by the Treaty of Le Goulet in 1200. In 1307 Philip IV gave it as an appanage to his half-brother Louis, whose son married Joan II of Navarre, founding the Évreux kings of Navarre.
county-of-evreux.e: Charles the Bad of Navarre used Évreux as a base for his intrigues against John II and Charles V, who seized most of his Norman lands. In 1404 his son Charles III of Navarre exchanged Évreux with Charles VI for the duchy of Nemours, and it returned to the Kingdom of France.

county-of-portugal.t: The county of Portucale between the Minho and Douro, founded with the capture of Porto in 868, from which the Kingdom of Portugal was born.
county-of-portugal.o: In 868 Vímara Peres, a vassal of Alfonso III of Asturias, took the town of Portucale (Porto) on the Douro and was made count of the region between the Minho and the Douro. His descendants governed it as a frontier county within the Kingdom of León, and Countess Mumadona Dias fortified Guimarães in the 10th century.
county-of-portugal.r: The counts ruled a mixed population of Galician-speaking peasants, resettled Mozarabs and frontier warriors. The county was abolished after García II of Galicia defeated Count Nuno Mendes in 1071. In 1096 Alfonso VI of León recreated it, now including Coimbra, for Henry of Burgundy, husband of his daughter Teresa, who ruled after Henry's death in 1112.
county-of-portugal.e: Teresa's son Afonso Henriques defeated her party at São Mamede in 1128. After his victory at Ourique in 1139 he took the title of king, recognised by León in 1143, and the county became the Kingdom of Portugal.

commune-of-cremona.t: A rich Po valley city-republic, usually loyal to the emperors and Milan's great rival, crowned by the Torrazzo bell tower.
commune-of-cremona.o: Cremona's citizens won rights from their bishop in the late 11th century, and consuls are recorded from 1098. Commanding a crossing of the Po, the city became a major river port and soon clashed with Milan and its ally Crema.
commune-of-cremona.r: Cremona was governed by consuls and later a podestà, with a strong guild of merchants and cloth makers. It generally sided with the emperors: it helped Frederick Barbarossa destroy Crema in 1160 and was a key base for Frederick II. The Torrazzo, one of the tallest medieval bell towers in Italy, and the cathedral date from this period. In the 13th century Ghibelline strongmen such as Buoso da Dovara and Uberto Pallavicino held power.
commune-of-cremona.e: Faction struggles between the Cavalcabò and their rivals weakened the commune, and in 1334 it submitted to Azzone Visconti, becoming part of the Lordship of Milan.

county-of-bigorre.t: Small Pyrenean county around Tarbes and Lourdes, remembered for one of the oldest charters of customs in France.
county-of-bigorre.o: Bigorre, the land of the ancient Bigerriones, became a county under the Carolingians in the 9th century, at the edge of the Duchy of Gascony. Its first counts are poorly documented, and their line was linked with the rulers of Gascony and Aragon.
county-of-bigorre.r: The county controlled the upper Adour valley and passes into Aragon, with Tarbes as its seat and the castle of Lourdes as its stronghold. The Fors de Bigorre, granted around 1097, set out the rights of the inhabitants and limits on comital power. In the 13th century Countess Petronilla married five times, leaving a bitter succession dispute.
county-of-bigorre.e: Bigorre passed through several hands, including English rule after 1360, before falling to the House of Foix-Béarn in the 15th century and then to the Albret kings of Navarre. When Henry of Navarre became Henry IV of France, it was united with the crown in 1607.

county-of-monzon.t: A Leonese frontier county on the Tierra de Campos, created for the Ansúrez family as a counterweight to Castile.
county-of-monzon.o: Around 943 Ramiro II of León created the County of Monzón, around Monzón de Campos near Palencia, for Assur Fernández, a rival of Fernán González of Castile. It was part of the king's effort to check the growing independence of Castile.
county-of-monzon.r: The Ansúrez counts governed a fertile plain of the Tierra de Campos, newly resettled by farmers, from the castle of Monzón. They were among the leading nobles of the Kingdom of León, involved in its civil wars and frontier fighting against the Caliphate of Córdoba.
county-of-monzon.e: After Fernando Ansúrez, the county passed by marriage and conflict into the hands of other families and was absorbed into the domains of the kings of León and Castile by the early 11th century. The Ansúrez family later produced Pedro Ansúrez, the lord who developed Valladolid.

coriondi.t: People of south-east Ireland known only from Ptolemy's Geography, whose name may be related to later Irish population names.
coriondi.o: The Coriondi appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, placed in the interior of south-eastern Ireland, roughly in modern Counties Kilkenny, Carlow or Wexford, near the Brigantes (Ireland) and the Usdiae. As with his other Irish peoples, his information came from earlier sailors' and traders' reports.
coriondi.r: Nothing is known of their government or way of life. Some scholars have compared their name with the Coraind, a group mentioned in early Irish texts, or with British names built on the element coria, meaning a war band or host, but no identification is certain.
coriondi.e: The Coriondi disappear from the record after Ptolemy. Their region later fell within the Kingdom of Leinster and the Kingdom of Osraige.
