chersonesus-taurica.t: Democratic Greek city in south-western Crimea, colony of Heraclea Pontica, whose ruins near Sevastopol preserve a whole ancient landscape of farm plots.
chersonesus-taurica.o: Colonists from Heraclea Pontica, joined according to tradition by settlers from Delos, founded Chersonesus in 422-421 BCE on a small bay in the south-west of Crimea, perhaps on the site of an earlier trading post. Over the 4th century BCE the city took control of the Heracleian peninsula and parts of the north-west Crimean coast.
chersonesus-taurica.r: Chersonesus was a democracy whose citizens swore an oath, preserved in a 3rd-century BCE inscription, to defend the city and never betray it. Its farmland was divided into regular rectangular plots, many planted with vineyards, and wine, fish and grain were its main exports. Its patron deity was the Maiden (Parthenos).
chersonesus-taurica.e: Pressed by the Scythians of Crimea under Scilurus and Palacus, the city appealed to Mithridates VI of Pontus c. 110 BCE; his general Diophantus defended it, and it passed under Pontic and later Roman protection. As Byzantine Cherson it survived into the Middle Ages, where tradition places the baptism of Vladimir of Kiev in 988.

coriosolites.t: Armorican people of northern Brittany, best known today for huge hoards of their distinctive billon coins found in Jersey.
coriosolites.o: The Coriosolites lived in the modern Côtes-d'Armor, around the Rance estuary. Caesar names them among the Armorican peoples who submitted to Publius Crassus in 57 BCE.
coriosolites.r: They issued abundant coins of base silver with stylised heads and horses. Hoards buried around the time of the Roman conquest, above all the Grouville hoard found in Jersey in 2012 with around 70,000 coins, suggest wealth from cross-Channel trade or refugees fleeing Caesar.
coriosolites.e: After joining the Veneti and the Unelli in 56 BCE they were absorbed into Gallia Lugdunensis. Their Roman capital was Fanum Martis at Corseul, with a large temple of Mars, and the name survives in Corseul.

county-of-louvain.t: The county around Leuven and Brussels from which the Reginarid counts built the Duchy of Brabant.
county-of-louvain.o: Around 1003 Lambert I the Bearded, a member of the Reginarid family, took the title of count of Louvain. He held lands around Leuven and Brussels, which was growing on the Senne, and expanded them through war with the bishops of Liège and neighbouring lords.
county-of-louvain.r: The counts ruled a fertile, densely settled region on the trade routes between the Rhine and Flanders. Brussels and Leuven grew as market towns. Godfrey I of Louvain was named duke of Lower Lorraine in 1106, giving the family the ducal title and a claim to authority over the whole region, and they also styled themselves landgraves of Brabant.
county-of-louvain.e: Around 1183 Count Henry I began using the title duke of Brabant, and after the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall in 1190 the county became the core of the Duchy of Brabant, whose dukes ruled from Brussels and Leuven.

county-of-vaudemont.t: A small Lorraine county held by a cadet line of the ducal house, whose heir René II finally inherited the Duchy of Lorraine itself.
county-of-vaudemont.o: Around 1070 Duke Gerard of Lorraine's younger son Gerard received the county of Vaudémont, south of Nancy, with its castle on the hill of Sion. His descendants ruled it as a cadet branch, often at odds with the main ducal line.
county-of-vaudemont.r: Vaudémont was a modest rural county whose hill of Sion was a Marian pilgrimage site. In the 14th century it passed to the house of Joinville and then, by marriage, to Ferry of Lorraine. His son Antoine of Vaudémont claimed the Duchy of Lorraine and defeated René of Anjou at Bulgnéville in 1431.
county-of-vaudemont.e: Antoine's son Ferry II married René's daughter Yolande, and their son René II inherited the Duchy of Lorraine in 1473, merging Vaudémont with it. The title survived as a dignity for younger members of the ducal family.

county-of-macon.t: Carolingian county in southern Burgundy, the land in which the great abbey of Cluny was founded in 910.
county-of-macon.o: The Mâconnais, around Mâcon on the Saône, became a Carolingian county in the 9th century, at the junction of the lands of West Francia and the Burgundian kingdoms. Its early counts were linked with the dukes of Aquitaine and Burgundy.
county-of-macon.r: In 910 Duke William I of Aquitaine founded the abbey of Cluny in the county, free from lay and episcopal control, and it became the head of a vast monastic network. From the late 10th century the county was held by a branch of the house of Burgundy-Ivrea descended from Otto-William, who also ruled the Free County of Burgundy.
county-of-macon.e: The last countess, Alix, and her husband John of Dreux sold the county to Louis IX of France in 1239, and it was attached to the royal domain. The Mâconnais remains known for its wines.

corcyra.t: Corinthian colony on Corfu that grew into a major naval power, whose clash with Corinth helped trigger the Peloponnesian War.
corcyra.o: Corinthians under Chersicrates founded Corcyra on the island of Corfu c. 733 BCE, displacing earlier Eretrian settlers. Its position on the route to Italy and Sicily made it rich, and it soon broke with its mother city: Thucydides dates the first Greek sea battle, between Corinth and Corcyra, to c. 664 BCE.
corcyra.r: Corcyra had the second-largest Greek navy by the 430s BCE. Its quarrel with Corinth over Epidamnus led to battles at Leukimme and Sybota and an alliance with Athens. A brutal civil war between democrats and oligarchs from 427 BCE is described by Thucydides. The temple of Artemis has the oldest stone Greek pediment, with a Gorgon.
corcyra.e: In the Hellenistic period Corcyra was held by Agathocles of Syracuse and Pyrrhus of the Kingdom of Epirus. After an Illyrian attack in 229 BCE, it placed itself under Roman protection, becoming a Roman ally and base.

celtici.t: Celtic communities of south-western Iberia, said by Pliny to have migrated from Celtiberia, living in the Alentejo and western Andalusia.
celtici.o: Strabo and Pliny describe Celtici in the south-west, between the Guadiana and the Atlantic and in the Beturia region of Extremadura and Huelva. Pliny says they came from the Celtiberians, as shown by their religion, language and town names, though the date of their arrival is uncertain, probably from the 5th century BCE.
celtici.r: They lived in fortified settlements such as Nertobriga and Mirobriga, whose -briga names are Celtic. Their society of farmers and herders lay close to the mining districts of the Sierra Morena. They seem to have been a group of communities rather than a single polity.
celtici.e: Their territory was drawn into Hispania Ulterior and was pacified after the Lusitanian wars and the campaigns of Decimus Junius Brutus from 138 BCE. Under Augustus it was split between Lusitania and Baetica.

cantiaci.t: The people of Kent, first named by Julius Caesar, whose four kings attacked his ships in 54 BCE and whose coast saw the Roman landing of 43.
cantiaci.o: Kent was the part of Britain closest to Gaul, and Caesar described its people as the most civilised of the Britons, much like the Gauls in custom. When he crossed in 55 and 54 BCE, Cantium was divided among four kings, Cingetorix, Carvilius, Taximagulus and Segovax, who attacked his beached fleet at the command of Cassivellaunus and were driven off.
cantiaci.r: Kent was densely farmed and closely tied to the Continent, receiving Gallo-Belgic coins and producing its own issues, including early cast potin coins. Oppida grew at Canterbury, Rochester and Bigbury. In the decades before the Claudian invasion, coins of Dubnovellaunus and later the influence of Cunobelinus of the Catuvellauni suggest Kent fell under the sway of more powerful northern neighbours.
cantiaci.e: The Roman army landed at Richborough in 43, and Kent was quickly absorbed into Roman Britain. Its people formed the civitas of the Cantiaci, governed from Durovernum Cantiacorum, the later Canterbury. The old name lived on in the Kingdom of Kent and the modern county.

county-of-chiny.t: A small Ardennes county on the Semois, on whose lands the Cistercian abbey of Orval was founded, before it was absorbed by Luxembourg.
county-of-chiny.o: The county emerged in the mid-10th century in the southern Ardennes, in the frontier region between the Lotharingian duchies and France. Its first known count, Otto of Warcq, built a castle at Chiny on the Semois, and his descendants extended their lands towards Ivoix and Montmédy.
county-of-chiny.r: Chiny was a wooded, thinly settled county of castles, iron working and abbeys. The counts sponsored the abbey of Orval, founded in 1070 and later Cistercian, which became the county's main religious centre. They were vassals of the Empire, connected by marriage to Bar, Namur and Loon.
county-of-chiny.e: In 1226 Countess Jeanne married Arnold of Loon, joining Chiny to the County of Loon. After the Loon line ended, the county was sold in 1364 to Wenceslaus, duke of Luxembourg, and merged into the County of Luxembourg; it lies today in Belgium.

commune-of-mantua.t: A lake-ringed city-republic of the Po plain that emerged after Matilda of Canossa's death and ended when the Bonacolsi seized power in 1272.
commune-of-mantua.o: Mantua had been a centre of Matilda of Canossa's lands. After her death in 1115 its citizens organised a commune under consuls, taking control of the city and the countryside from the old feudal lords and the bishop.
commune-of-mantua.r: The commune was governed by consuls and later a podestà. Mantua joined the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa and in the late 12th century engineer Alberto Pitentino regulated the Mincio to form the lakes that still surround the city. Mantua traded along the Po and the Mincio and fought neighbours such as Verona and Cremona. The troubadour poet Sordello came from its territory.
commune-of-mantua.e: In 1272 Pinamonte Bonacolsi made himself captain of the people and ruled as lord, ending communal government. The Gonzaga overthrew the Bonacolsi in 1328, founding what became the Duchy of Mantua.

canton-of-valencia.t: A federalist canton proclaimed in Valencia during the Cantonal Rebellion of 1873 and suppressed within weeks.
canton-of-valencia.o: In July 1873 radical federalists in Valencia, frustrated by the Spanish First Republic's failure to build a federal state, formed a revolutionary junta and proclaimed the city a sovereign canton, joining the rising begun in the Canton of Cartagena.
canton-of-valencia.r: The junta took over city government and local forces and declared its intention to belong to a federal Spain built by free cantons. Like the other cantons, it had little time to put any programme into practice.
canton-of-valencia.e: Government troops under General Arsenio Martínez Campos besieged and bombarded the city, and the canton surrendered in early August 1873.

ciarraige-luachra.t: North Kerry kingdom of the Ciarraige, the people who gave County Kerry its name, later ruled by the O'Connor Kerry family.
ciarraige-luachra.o: The Ciarraige, 'people of Ciar', were one of several groups of that name in early Ireland, claiming descent from a legendary ancestor Ciar. The Ciarraige Luachra held north Kerry around Tralee and the Feale valley from the early medieval period, as a subject people paying tribute to the Eóganachta kings of the Kingdom of Munster.
ciarraige-luachra.r: Their kingdom was a land of bog, upland and coastal plain, and its wealth lay in cattle. St Brendan the Navigator, founder of Clonfert, was traditionally born among them near Tralee, and the region had a lively church life. Their kings, from the 11th century known as Ó Conchobhair Chiarraí, O'Connor Kerry, held a respected place among the lesser kings of Munster.
ciarraige-luachra.e: In the 13th century Anglo-Norman lords, especially the FitzGeralds, took much of their land, and the O'Connors Kerry were confined to the north of the county, in Iraghticonnor, ruled from Carrigafoyle Castle until the late 16th century. The people's name lives on in County Kerry.

commune-of-san-gimignano.t: A small Tuscan hill-town republic on the pilgrim road to Rome, whose surviving medieval towers make it the best-preserved image of a communal city.
commune-of-san-gimignano.o: San Gimignano grew on the Via Francigena, the pilgrim route from northern Europe to Rome, and won self-government from the bishops of Volterra; by 1199 it was an independent commune under consuls.
commune-of-san-gimignano.r: The town prospered from pilgrims, trade and especially saffron, grown in the surrounding hills and sold as far as Egypt and Syria. Rival families, led by the Ardinghelli and the Salvucci, built tower houses as symbols of wealth and power; around 72 are said to have stood, and 14 survive. Dante came as an envoy of Florence in 1300. The Collegiata church was frescoed by Sienese painters.
commune-of-san-gimignano.e: The Black Death of 1348 and the decline of the pilgrim trade left the town poor and exhausted by feuds. In 1353 it submitted to the Republic of Florence, and its towers survived because it stopped growing.

commune-of-modena.t: An Emilian city-republic whose Romanesque cathedral is a masterpiece of medieval sculpture, and Bologna's lasting rival on the Via Emilia.
commune-of-modena.o: Modena had belonged to the lands of Matilda of Canossa, and its cathedral was begun in 1099 by the architect Lanfranco with sculpture by Wiligelmo. After Matilda's death the citizens organised a commune, with consuls recorded by 1135.
commune-of-modena.r: The commune was governed by consuls, later a podestà and popular councils. Modena was usually Ghibelline and fought a long rivalry with Guelph Bologna over borders and water rights in the plain. Its cathedral and the Ghirlandina bell tower became symbols of civic identity. Factional wars between noble families, the Grasolfi and Aigoni, crippled the government in the later 13th century.
commune-of-modena.e: In 1288 the city gave lordship to Obizzo II d'Este of the Duchy of Ferrara. Apart from brief interruptions, the Este held Modena from then on, and it later became the capital of the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

consoranni.t: Pyrenean people of the upper Salat valley who gave their name to the Couserans district of the Ariège.
consoranni.o: Known from Pliny and later Roman sources, the Consoranni lived in the central Pyrenees in the modern Ariège, between the Convenae and the Volcae Tectosages. Little else is recorded of them before the Roman conquest.
consoranni.r: No rulers or institutions are known.
consoranni.e: Their land came under Roman control during the conquest of Aquitania. Their chief town, Lugdunum Consoranorum, later took the name of a bishop, Saint-Lizier, and the region kept the name Couserans.

corcu-loigde.t: Kingdom of the Érainn in south-west Cork, ancestral to the O'Driscolls, which tradition remembers as rulers of Munster before the Eóganachta.
corcu-loigde.o: The Corcu Loigde were a people of the Érainn, the old population group of Munster linked with the Iverni of Ptolemy. In Irish tradition they held the kingship of Munster before the rise of the Eóganachta of Cashel around the 5th century, and afterwards kept a respected place as a free subject kingdom in south-west Cork.
corcu-loigde.r: Their kingdom covered the coast and hinterland from around Clonakilty to Baltimore and inland toward Skibbereen. St Ciarán of Saigir, among the earliest Irish saints, was claimed as one of their kin, and a genealogical text on the Corcu Loigde preserves their lineages. The ruling family became known as Ó hEidirsceoil, later O'Driscoll, with power based on cattle, farmland and the sea.
corcu-loigde.e: From the 12th century the MacCarthys of Desmond and then the Anglo-Normans pushed the Corcu Loigde to the coast. The O'Driscolls survived as lords of Collymore around Baltimore and its islands until the early 17th century.

caere.t: Coastal Etruscan city, now Cerveteri, famed for its vast tomb-city of the Banditaccia and its ports open to Greek and Phoenician traders.
caere.o: Caere, Etruscan Caisra, Greek Agylla, rose on a tufa plateau near the Tyrrhenian coast north-west of Rome. Villanovan villages united into a city during the 8th century BCE, and by the 7th century the princely Regolini-Galassi tomb shows great wealth from metals and long-distance trade.
caere.r: Caere looked to the sea through its ports, Pyrgi, Alsium and Punicum. At Pyrgi the gold tablets of about 500 BCE, written in Etruscan and Phoenician, record king Thefarie Velianas dedicating a shrine to the goddess Uni-Astarte. Caere joined Carthage against the Phocaean Greeks at Alalia around 540 BCE, kept a treasury at Delphi and produced painted Caeretan hydriae and the famous Sarcophagus of the Spouses.
caere.e: Caere was long on friendly terms with Rome, sheltering Roman sacred objects during the Gallic sack of 390 BCE and receiving a form of citizenship without the vote. After a brief revolt it lost half its territory in 273 BCE and became a Roman town. Its necropolises are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

caeroesi.t: One of the Germani Cisrhenani of the Ardennes and Eifel, who joined the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE.
caeroesi.o: Caesar names the Caeroesi with the Condrusi, Eburones and Paemani as peoples called Germani living west of the Rhine. They are usually placed in the Eifel, between the Treveri and the Eburones.
caeroesi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or settlements.
caeroesi.e: In 57 BCE they promised, together with the other Germani Cisrhenani, some forty thousand warriors to the Belgic league against Caesar. After the conquest they vanish from the record, their land probably absorbed by the Treveri or the Tungri.

county-of-tusculum.t: Lordship of the Counts of Tusculum, a Roman noble family who controlled the papacy in the early 11th century and fought the commune of Rome.
county-of-tusculum.o: The counts of Tusculum descended from the Theophylacti, the family that dominated Rome in the 10th century. Around 999 Gregory I of Tusculum held the fortified hill town of Tusculum in the Alban Hills, and from there his family built a lordship over the countryside south-east of Rome.
county-of-tusculum.r: The Tusculani controlled papal elections for decades: Gregory's sons became Popes Benedict VIII (1012–1024) and John XIX (1024–1032), and his grandson Benedict IX was pope three times before being removed. Their power declined after the reform papacy and the Roman commune emerged, but in 1167 Tusculan troops and imperial forces routed a Roman army at Monte Porzio.
county-of-tusculum.e: Squeezed between Rome and the papacy, the counts placed Tusculum under papal and imperial protection in the 12th century. In 1191 the Romans, with Emperor Henry VI's consent, destroyed the town. Survivors are said to have founded nearby Frascati.

ce.t: A Pictish province named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne, probably in Mar and Buchan in north-east Scotland.
ce.o: Ce is listed among the seven Pictish provinces, named after the sons of Cruithne. It is usually placed in Aberdeenshire, around Mar and Buchan, partly because the hill Bennachie may preserve its name.
ce.r: Nothing is known of its rulers or institutions. The area is rich in Pictish symbol stones and hillforts, such as Bennachie's Mither Tap, suggesting an organised society within the wider Pictish kingdom.
ce.e: Ce disappeared as a distinct unit when Pictland became part of the Kingdom of Scotland. The later mormaerdoms or earldoms of Mar and Buchan may continue its territory.

county-of-perigord.t: Medieval county of the Dordogne valley around Périgueux, the land of the ancient Petrocorii.
county-of-perigord.o: In 866 Charles the Bald entrusted the counties of Périgord and Angoulême to Vulgrin, a kinsman, to resist Viking raids along the rivers of western France. After his death the two counties were divided between his sons, and Périgord passed to a line of counts from whom the later Talleyrand-Périgord family claimed descent.
county-of-perigord.r: The counts were vassals of the Duchy of Aquitaine and held a land of castles and abbeys on the frontier between English and French power. Their authority was contested by the burghers of Périgueux, whose town of Puy-Saint-Front won wide privileges.
county-of-perigord.e: During the Hundred Years' War the counts changed sides repeatedly. In 1399 Count Archambaud VI was condemned for treason and his county confiscated; Charles VI gave it in 1400 to his brother Louis of Orléans. It later passed to the Albret family and was united with the crown under Henry IV.

carnonacae.t: People of north-west Scotland named in Ptolemy's Geography, usually placed on the coast of Wester Ross.
carnonacae.o: The Carnonacae appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the western coast of the Scottish Highlands, north of the Creones and south of the Caereni, roughly in modern Wester Ross. Their name may contain a Celtic element meaning cairn or horn, perhaps referring to rocky headlands.
carnonacae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions. The coast of Wester Ross supported small populations living in roundhouses and duns, with brochs appearing along the Atlantic seaboard in the last centuries BCE. These tall drystone towers suggest local elites able to organise considerable labour.
carnonacae.e: The Carnonacae do not appear in any later source. Their territory later formed part of the lands of the Picts and, from the 9th century, came under strong Norse influence.

county-of-nevers.t: A Loire county in Burgundy's orbit that passed through Flemish, Burgundian and Cleves hands before becoming a duchy in 1539.
county-of-nevers.o: Around 990 Otto-William, count of Burgundy, gave the county of Nevers to his son-in-law Landry, who founded its first dynasty. Landry's descendants also held Auxerre and Tonnerre, giving the counts a large lordship along the upper Loire and the Yonne.
county-of-nevers.r: Nevers lay on the Loire between the royal domain and the Duchy of Burgundy, with forests, ironworks and river trade. Several counts went on crusade, and Count William III joined the Second Crusade. In the 13th and 14th centuries the county passed by marriage to the Flemish counts, including Louis of Nevers, and then to a younger branch of the Valois dukes of Burgundy.
county-of-nevers.e: In 1491 it passed to the house of Cleves, and in 1539 Francis I raised it to a duchy-peerage for François de Clèves. The Duchy of Nevers later went to the Gonzagas and the Mazarins, and lost its last rights in the Revolution.

callatis.t: Dorian colony of Heraclea Pontica on the Dobruja coast, a grain-trading city that defied Lysimachus and later allied with Rome, at modern Mangalia.
callatis.o: Callatis was founded by colonists from Heraclea Pontica on the western Black Sea coast, probably in the late 6th century BCE, though some sources place the foundation later. Its fertile hinterland in southern Dobruja made it a natural centre for grain exports, and it grew alongside the Milesian colonies of Histria, Tomis and Odessos.
callatis.r: Callatis kept the Doric dialect and institutions of its mother city, with cults of Apollo, Dionysus and Heracles. It traded grain, wine and craft goods with the Getae of the interior and struck its own coinage. In 313 BCE it led the Pontic cities in revolt against Lysimachus, withstanding a long siege that ended around 309 BCE.
callatis.e: In the 1st century BCE Callatis concluded a formal treaty with Rome, a rare surviving text of its kind. After the campaign of Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus in 72-71 BCE it lay within the Roman sphere and later in the province of Moesia. The site is the modern Romanian town of Mangalia.

county-of-rodez.t: The county of the Rouergue around Rodez, held by the Millau and Armagnac families, which shared its hilltop city with a powerful bishop.
county-of-rodez.o: The county of Rouergue had belonged to the counts of Toulouse. In 1112 the viscount of Millau, Richard, acquired the county of Rodez, founding a local line that ruled the comital part of the city, the Bourg, while the bishop governed the Cité around the cathedral.
county-of-rodez.r: The Rouergue was a land of uplands, sheep and pilgrim routes to Compostela, with Conques nearby. Count Henry II of Rodez was a patron of troubadours in the late 13th century. In 1302 his daughter Cécile brought Rodez to Bernard VI of Armagnac, and the county became one of the Armagnacs' chief holdings.
county-of-rodez.e: After the Armagnac line ended, Rodez passed to the Alençon and Albret families and so to Henry of Navarre. When he became Henry IV in 1589, the county joined the Kingdom of France; his personal lands were formally united with the crown in 1607.

county-of-besalu.t: A small Catalan county of the Garrotxa whose fortified bridge and Jewish quarter still mark the medieval town of Besalú.
county-of-besalu.o: Besalú emerged as a county in the later 9th century, carved out of the lands of Girona and linked to the family of Wilfred the Hairy. For much of the 10th century it was held together with Cerdanya by Wilfred's descendants, before acquiring its own line of counts.
county-of-besalu.r: Its best-known count, Bernat I Tallaferro, from 988 to 1020, was a brother of Abbot Oliba and briefly obtained a bishopric for Besalú from the pope in 1017. The town grew around its castle, monasteries such as Sant Pere de Besalú, a fortified bridge over the Fluvià and a Jewish community whose ritual bath survives. The economy was rural, with markets on the routes to Roussillon.
county-of-besalu.e: Count Bernat III married a daughter of Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona and died without heirs in 1111, so the county passed to Barcelona. It became part of Catalonia and the Crown of Aragon.

county-of-armagnac.t: A Gascon county whose counts gave their name to a faction in France's civil war and fought Louis XI to the bitter end.
county-of-armagnac.o: Armagnac was carved out of the duchy of Gascony around 960 for Bernard the Squinter, a younger son of the Gascon ducal house. His descendants ruled the hill country around Auch and Lectoure and gradually gathered neighbouring counties such as Fezensac and Rodez.
county-of-armagnac.r: The counts were among the greatest lords of the south-west, shifting between the English in Guyenne and the French crown. Bernard VII became constable of France and led the Armagnac party against the Burgundians in the civil war of the 1410s until his murder in Paris in 1418. The land was known for wine and its brandy, later named after it.
county-of-armagnac.e: Count John V defied Louis XI and was killed when royal troops took Lectoure in 1473. The last count, Charles I, died in 1497, and the county passed to the duke of Alençon and later to the house of Albret before returning to the Kingdom of France.

county-of-ribagorza.t: A Pyrenean county between Aragon and Catalonia, with its bishopric at Roda de Isábena, later absorbed into the Kingdom of Aragon.
county-of-ribagorza.o: Ribagorza, the valleys of the Isábena and Noguera Ribagorzana, was part of the Frankish County of Toulouse until around 872, when Ramon I established himself as count of Pallars and Ribagorza. After his death Ribagorza went to one of his sons.
county-of-ribagorza.r: The counts ruled a mountain society of herders and farmers, defended by castles against the Muslim lords of Lleida and Barbastro. They founded a bishopric at Roda de Isábena, whose cathedral was consecrated in 956, making it the county's religious centre. The county shared its culture and language with both Aragon and Catalonia.
county-of-ribagorza.e: Almanzor's raids weakened the county around 1000. Sancho III of Navarre took control in the 1010s and 1020s, and in 1035 Ribagorza passed with Sobrarbe to his son Gonzalo. After Gonzalo's death around 1045 it went to Ramiro I, joining the Kingdom of Aragon.

convenae.t: Mixed community gathered by Pompey in the central Pyrenees, whose town became Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges.
convenae.o: Their name means those who came together. According to Jerome, around 72 BCE Pompey, returning from his war against Sertorius in Hispania, settled defeated fighters and mountain people at Lugdunum in the upper Garonne valley.
convenae.r: The community mixed Iberian, Aquitanian and Roman elements and quickly adopted Roman ways. Its town had a forum, temple, baths and theatre.
convenae.e: Their land was absorbed into Roman Aquitania; Caesar's legate Crassus campaigned in the region in 56 BCE. Lugdunum Convenarum became Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges, with its Romanesque cathedral, and the region kept the name Comminges.

crown-of-castile.t: The union of Castile and León that conquered most of al-Andalus, sent Columbus across the Atlantic and formed the core of the Spanish monarchy.
crown-of-castile.o: In 1230 Ferdinand III, king of the Kingdom of Castile, inherited the Kingdom of León, permanently uniting the two crowns. He then conquered Córdoba in 1236, Jaén in 1246 and Seville in 1248, leaving only the Emirate of Granada as a Muslim state.
crown-of-castile.r: Castile's Cortes, wool trade dominated by the Mesta, towns and military orders shaped its society. Alfonso X sponsored law codes and translations at Toledo. The Trastámara dynasty took power in 1369. Isabella I and Ferdinand II conquered Granada in 1492, the same year Columbus sailed, and the Inquisition and expulsion of the Jews followed.
crown-of-castile.e: From 1516 Castile was the heartland of Habsburg Spain, supplying its taxes, soldiers and American empire. After the War of the Spanish Succession, the Nueva Planta decrees imposed Castilian institutions on Aragon, and the Crown merged into a unified Spanish state.

county-of-pallars-sobira.t: A remote Pyrenean county around Sort whose counts kept a degree of independence until 1491, the last of the old Catalan counties to be extinguished.
county-of-pallars-sobira.o: It was formed in 1011 when Count Sunyer of Pallars divided his lands between his sons. Guillem II received the high valleys of the Noguera Pallaresa around Sort and the Àneu valleys, while his brother Ramon III took the lower County of Pallars Jussà.
county-of-pallars-sobira.r: A mountain land of pastures, iron and small villages, Pallars Sobirà was ruled by a line of counts from Sort and the castle of Valencia d'Àneu. They became vassals of the Counts of Barcelona and later the Crown of Aragon, but kept wide local powers. Many bore the names Artau and Hug Roger.
county-of-pallars-sobira.e: Count Hug Roger III sided against King John II in the Catalan civil war of 1462-1472 and later resisted Ferdinand II. Defeated in 1487, he lost his county, which was confiscated in 1491 and given to the Cardona family as the Marquisate of Pallars.

carausian-empire.t: Breakaway Roman regime in Britain and northern Gaul, founded by the admiral Carausius in 286, the first time Britain was ruled as a separate realm.
carausian-empire.o: Carausius, a Menapian from the Low Countries, commanded the Roman fleet charged with clearing Frankish and Saxon pirates from the Channel. Accused of keeping captured plunder for himself and sentenced to death by Maximian, he declared himself emperor in 286, taking control of Britain and part of northern Gaul with his fleet.
carausian-empire.r: Carausius ruled from London and Boulogne, presenting himself as a legitimate colleague of Diocletian and Maximian. His coins, minted at London and another British mint, carried slogans such as RESTITVTOR BRITANNIAE and EXPECTATE VENI, quoting Virgil. He kept a strong fleet, repelled Maximian's attempted invasion in 289 and may have begun forts of the Saxon Shore.
carausian-empire.e: In 293 Constantius Chlorus captured Boulogne, and Carausius was murdered by his finance minister Allectus, who took power. In 296 Constantius invaded; his prefect Asclepiodotus defeated and killed Allectus, and Constantius entered London, as the Arras medallion celebrates. Britain returned to Roman Britain.

county-of-forez.t: A county of the upper Loire, ruled from Montbrison, that separated from Lyon in 1173 and passed to the dukes of Bourbon.
county-of-forez.o: In the 10th and 11th centuries a single family held the counties of Lyon and Forez, contesting control of Lyon with its archbishops. The register dates the county from around 1000. By the 1173 agreement known as the Permutatio, Count Guy II gave up his rights in Lyon to the archbishop and kept Forez.
county-of-forez.r: The counts ruled from Montbrison over a land of plains and hills on the upper Loire, founding towns and abbeys. They cultivated close ties with the French crown and with the lords of Beaujeu. The county's customs and archives are unusually well preserved, including the 15th-century Armorial of Forez.
county-of-forez.e: In 1371 the heiress Anne of Forez married Louis II, Duke of Bourbon, and the county joined the Duchy of Bourbon. After Francis I confiscated the lands of Constable Charles of Bourbon, Forez was united with the Kingdom of France in 1531.

chalcedon.t: Megarian colony on the Asian shore of the Bosporus, mocked as the 'city of the blind' for overlooking the better site of Byzantium opposite.
chalcedon.o: Settlers from Megara founded Chalcedon c. 685 BCE on the Asian side of the Bosporus, opposite the later site of Byzantium. Herodotus reports the Persian Megabazus calling its founders blind for choosing the poorer site when the better one lay across the strait.
chalcedon.r: Chalcedon lived from farming, fishing and Bosporus traffic, though Byzantium controlled the main currents. It came under the Achaemenid Empire, then paid tribute in the Delian League. The sophist Thrasymachus came from Chalcedon. In the Hellenistic period it was closely tied to Byzantium and pressed by the Kingdom of Bithynia.
chalcedon.e: When Nicomedes IV left Bithynia to Rome in 74 BCE, Chalcedon passed under Roman rule; Mithridates defeated a Roman force there that year. It later hosted the Council of Chalcedon of 451 CE and is now Kadıköy in Istanbul.

carvetii.t: People of the Eden valley in Cumbria, known almost entirely from Roman inscriptions naming their self-governing civitas at Carlisle.
carvetii.o: The Carvetii lived in the Eden valley and around Carlisle in what is now Cumbria. They are not named by any ancient historian, and they may originally have been a section of the Brigantes that the Romans recognised as a separate community after the conquest of the north in the 70s.
carvetii.r: Their existence is known from inscriptions: a milestone of 223 from near Brougham names the civitas Carvetiorum, and a tombstone from Old Penrith records a councillor of the Carvetii. These show a self-governing community with a council, administered from Luguvalium, Carlisle, close to Hadrian's Wall. The countryside was farmed by native communities living in enclosed settlements.
carvetii.e: As one of the northernmost civitates of Roman Britain, the community lasted until Roman rule ended around 410. Carlisle remained an important centre afterwards, and the area later formed part of British kingdoms such as Rheged.

county-of-comminges.t: A Pyrenean county around Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges whose counts fought on the Occitan side in the Albigensian Crusade.
county-of-comminges.o: Counts of Comminges appear in the early 10th century, governing the upper Garonne valley around the old Roman town of Lugdunum Convenarum, later Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges. They were related to the counts of Couserans and Carcassonne and drifted into the orbit of the counts of Toulouse.
county-of-comminges.r: Comminges was a mountainous land of pastoral farming, small towns and pilgrimage, centred on the cathedral of Saint-Bertrand. The counts later held Muret near Toulouse. Count Bernard IV joined Raymond VI of Toulouse against the crusaders and was present at the battle of Muret in 1213, where Peter II of Aragon was killed.
county-of-comminges.e: The comital line ended with Countess Marguerite, whose disputed inheritance was settled in favour of the crown; Charles VII annexed Comminges to the Kingdom of France in 1454. The name survives as a region of the Haute-Garonne.

county-of-sobrarbe.t: A small Pyrenean county in northern Aragon, later the subject of the legend of the Fueros de Sobrarbe, the supposed oldest Aragonese laws.
county-of-sobrarbe.o: Sobrarbe, the valleys of the upper Cinca around Boltaña and Aínsa, emerged as a district in the 9th century under the shadow of Frankish power and of the neighbouring County of Ribagorza. Its early history is very poorly documented.
county-of-sobrarbe.r: Little is known of its government beyond its links with Ribagorza and the castles that defended it against the Muslim lords of Barbastro and Huesca. Its people were herders and farmers in the mountain valleys.
county-of-sobrarbe.e: Sancho III of Navarre took control in the early 11th century. On his death in 1035 Sobrarbe and Ribagorza went to his son Gonzalo, and after Gonzalo's murder around 1045 they passed to Ramiro I of Aragon, becoming part of the Kingdom of Aragon. Later writers invented a Kingdom of Sobrarbe with ancient fueros.

county-palatine-of-pembroke.t: A Norman marcher lordship in south-west Wales, base of Strongbow's invasion of Ireland and birthplace of Henry VII.
county-palatine-of-pembroke.o: Arnulf de Montgomery built the first castle at Pembroke in 1093, and it held out against Welsh counter-attacks. In 1138 King Stephen made Gilbert de Clare Earl of Pembroke, giving the lordship palatine powers. English and Flemish settlers occupied south Pembrokeshire, creating the 'Little England beyond Wales'.
county-palatine-of-pembroke.r: The earls exercised royal-style jurisdiction within the county. Gilbert's son Richard de Clare, Strongbow, led the invasion of Ireland in 1170 from here. William Marshal, who married Strongbow's heiress, rebuilt Pembroke Castle with its great round keep. Later holders included the Valence and Hastings families and Jasper Tudor, whose nephew Henry VII was born in the castle in 1457.
county-palatine-of-pembroke.e: The Laws in Wales Act of 1536 ended its special status, and Pembroke became the core of Pembrokeshire. The earldom title continued in the Herbert family.

catalan-republic-1641.t: A Catalan republic proclaimed during the Reapers' War, which lasted barely a week before Catalonia placed itself under the French king.
catalan-republic-1641.o: Catalonia rose against Philip IV in 1640 in the Reapers' War, provoked by the billeting of royal troops and the Count-Duke of Olivares's demands. As a royal army advanced on Barcelona, Pau Claris, president of the Generalitat, proclaimed a Catalan Republic under French protection in January 1641.
catalan-republic-1641.r: The republic was an emergency regime run by the Generalitat and Barcelona's councils, preoccupied with defence. Unable to resist Castilian forces alone, its leaders quickly decided that French support required a monarch.
catalan-republic-1641.e: On 23 January 1641 the Catalan authorities recognised Louis XIII of France as Count of Barcelona, ending the republic. Days later Catalan and French troops defeated the royal army at Montjuïc. Claris died in February, and Catalonia returned to Philip IV's rule in 1652, losing Roussillon to France in 1659.

county-of-roussillon.t: A Catalan county north of the Pyrenees centred on Perpignan, bequeathed to the Crown of Aragon in 1172 and French since 1659.
county-of-roussillon.o: Roussillon, named after the ancient town of Ruscino, became a Carolingian county in the early 9th century, part of the Marca Hispanica. It was long held with Empúries by a single comital family descended from Sunyer, until the two were divided in 991 and Roussillon got its own line of counts.
county-of-roussillon.r: The counts ruled from Perpignan, which grew into a prosperous town on the route between Catalonia and Languedoc. The economy rested on the fertile plain of the Têt, cloth making and trade. The county shared the Catalan language and laws, and monasteries such as Sant Miquel de Cuixà flourished in its hills.
county-of-roussillon.e: The last count, Girard II, died without heirs in 1172 and left Roussillon to Alfonso II of Aragon and Barcelona. It later formed part of the Kingdom of Majorca, and the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 gave it to France.

commune-of-arezzo.t: A Ghibelline city-republic of eastern Tuscany whose defeat at Campaldino in 1289 began its long decline before the power of Florence.
commune-of-arezzo.o: Arezzo, an old Etruscan and Roman town, was dominated by its powerful bishops, but consuls appear by 1098. The commune grew in the 12th century, contesting control of the town and the rural castles with the bishops and with neighbouring Siena.
commune-of-arezzo.r: Governed by consuls, then a podestà and later priors, Arezzo was generally Ghibelline. Its bishops remained political leaders: Guglielmino degli Ubertini died fighting Florence at Campaldino in 1289, and Guido Tarlati, bishop and lord from 1312 to 1327, expanded the city's territory and rebuilt its walls. The poet Petrarch was born in the city in 1304, his family having been exiled from Florence.
commune-of-arezzo.e: After Tarlati's death the city fell under outside lords and was racked by faction. In 1384 the French captain Enguerrand de Coucy sold it to the Republic of Florence, which ruled it for the rest of its history.

catana.t: Chalcidian Greek city at the foot of Mount Etna, home of the lawgiver Charondas, which was twice emptied of its people by Sicilian tyrants.
catana.o: Chalcidian colonists from Naxos founded Catana in 729 BCE, led by Euarchus, on the coast south of Mount Etna, in a fertile plain watered by the Simeto. The site had a good harbour and access to the Sicel interior.
catana.r: Catana was known for the laws of Charondas, adopted by other Chalcidian cities in Sicily and southern Italy. In 476 BCE Hieron I of Syracuse moved its people to Leontini, resettled it with Dorians and renamed it Aetna, celebrated by Pindar and Aeschylus; the original citizens returned in 461 BCE. It served as Athens' base during the Sicilian Expedition in 415 BCE. Its farmland and wine benefited from Etna's volcanic soil, though eruptions repeatedly struck it.
catana.e: In 403 BCE Dionysius I captured Catana and sold its people into slavery, settling Campanian mercenaries there. It recovered under later rulers and in 263 BCE was one of the first Sicilian cities taken by Rome, which carried off its sundial. Roman Catina became a prosperous town, today Catania.

county-of-maine.t: A county around Le Mans, long fought over by Anjou and Normandy, which became part of the Plantagenet heartland and later a royal appanage.
county-of-maine.o: Counts of Maine appear in the mid-10th century, ruling from Le Mans between the stronger principalities of Anjou, Normandy and Brittany. Count Herbert I, known as Wakedog, defended it against Fulk Nerra of Anjou in the early 11th century.
county-of-maine.r: Maine was a land of farming and forests, with a strong bishop and an assertive town: Le Mans formed one of the first urban communes in France around 1070. William the Conqueror took the county in 1063, but Count Elias of La Flèche recovered it, and his daughter's marriage to Fulk V joined it to Anjou.
county-of-maine.e: After Philip II seized it in 1204, Maine became part of the royal domain and was granted as an appanage to the Anjou princes. On the death of Charles of Maine in 1481 it returned permanently to the Kingdom of France.

commune-of-orvieto.t: A Guelph hill-town republic on a volcanic crag in Umbria, a frequent papal residence and builder of one of Italy's most splendid Gothic cathedrals.
commune-of-orvieto.o: Orvieto, perched on a tufa cliff above the Paglia valley, had consuls by 1157. The commune extended its rule over much of the surrounding countryside towards Lake Bolsena and the Tuscan Maremma.
commune-of-orvieto.r: Orvieto was ruled by consuls, then a podestà and a popular government of the Seven. Strongly Guelph, it often hosted popes in the 13th century, including Urban IV, at whose court Thomas Aquinas taught. The cathedral, begun in 1290, was linked to the Eucharistic miracle of Bolsena and the feast of Corpus Christi; Luca Signorelli later painted its frescoes. The Guelph Monaldeschi and Ghibelline Filippeschi, both named by Dante, fought for control.
commune-of-orvieto.e: Weakened by faction and the Black Death, the commune fell to strongmen in the 1340s. In 1354 Cardinal Albornoz restored papal authority, and Orvieto remained part of the Papal States.

county-of-provence.t: The Mediterranean county between the Rhône and the Alps that passed from Catalan to Angevin counts and was bequeathed to France in 1481.
county-of-provence.o: Under the kings of Arles, Boso of Arles held comital power in Provence around the mid-10th century. His son William the Liberator drove the Saracens from their base at Fraxinetum in 973 and became effective ruler of the region, founding the first comital dynasty.
county-of-provence.r: In 1112 the heiress Douce married Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona, bringing Catalan counts who fostered troubadour culture and Mediterranean trade. Raymond Berengar IV's daughter Beatrice married Charles of Anjou in 1246, and the Angevin counts, also kings of Naples, ruled from Aix and Naples. The popes settled at Avignon, on the county's edge, in the 14th century.
county-of-provence.e: Queen Joanna I adopted Louis I of Anjou, whose line held Provence until 1481. That year Charles of Maine, heir of René of Anjou, bequeathed it to Louis XI, and Provence was united with the Kingdom of France, while keeping its own estates and parliament at Aix.

clazomenae.t: Ionian city on the Gulf of Smyrna, birthplace of the philosopher Anaxagoras, which moved onto an offshore islet to escape Persian attack.
clazomenae.o: Clazomenae was founded by Ionian settlers, traditionally from Colophon, on the southern shore of the Gulf of Smyrna c. 1000 BCE. It joined the Ionian League and in the 7th century BCE helped found Abdera, a first attempt later renewed by Teos, and traded at Naucratis in Egypt.
clazomenae.r: Clazomenae was known for painted terracotta sarcophagi and olive oil. After the Ionian Revolt its people moved to an islet just offshore for safety. Anaxagoras, who taught that mind orders the cosmos, was born there c. 500 BCE. It belonged to the Delian League and was fought over during the Peloponnesian War.
clazomenae.e: The King's Peace of 387 BCE named Clazomenae as Persian territory. Alexander linked the island to the mainland by a causeway. Under Hellenistic kings and then Rome, from 133 BCE in the province of Asia, it slowly declined.

carnutes.t: Gallic people of the middle Loire, whose land held the annual assembly of the druids and whose massacre at Cenabum began the revolt of 52 BCE.
carnutes.o: The Carnutes lived between the Seine and the Loire, around Autricum (Chartres) and Cenabum (Orléans). Caesar reports that their territory was considered the centre of all Gaul, where the druids met each year in a sacred place to judge disputes.
carnutes.r: They were ruled by a nobility, and Caesar installed Tasgetius as their king, but he was murdered in 54 BCE. Cenabum, on the Loire, was a busy trading town where Roman merchants lived.
carnutes.e: In early 52 BCE the Carnutes killed the Roman traders at Cenabum, the signal for the revolt of Vercingetorix. Caesar sacked the town and in 51 BCE executed their leader Gutuater. Under Rome Autricum became Chartres and Cenabum was refounded as Aurelianum, later Orléans.

commune-of-treviso.t: The city-republic at the heart of the 'joyful March', whose courtly culture under the da Camino lords was praised by Dante.
commune-of-treviso.o: Treviso, north of Venice, had a commune of consuls in the 12th century and joined the Veronese League in 1164 and then the Lombard League. It dominated the March of Treviso, a region of rivers and fertile plain between the Alps and the lagoon.
commune-of-treviso.r: The commune was governed by consuls and later a podestà. Under Ezzelino III da Romano's brother Alberico it suffered harsh rule until 1259. The da Camino family then dominated; Gherardo da Camino, lord from 1283 to 1306, kept a brilliant court that Dante praised, and the region's festive life earned it the name Marca gioiosa. Treviso traded with Venice and the Alpine valleys.
commune-of-treviso.e: Cangrande della Scala took Treviso in 1329, joining it to the Lordship of Verona. In 1339 it submitted to the Republic of Venice, its first major mainland possession, which held it until 1797.

cenel-loairn.t: A leading kindred of Dal Riata in northern Argyll, rivals of Cenel nGabrain, whose descendants may later have ruled Moray.
cenel-loairn.o: Cenel Loairn claimed descent from Loarn mac Eirc, said to be a brother of Fergus Mor, the legendary founder of Dal Riata. By the 7th century it controlled Lorn, Mull and neighbouring districts in northern Argyll, with its main stronghold at Dunollie near Oban.
cenel-loairn.r: Like other Dal Riatan kindreds it owed naval service and tribute recorded in the Senchus fer nAlban. Its kings competed with Cenel nGabrain for the kingship of all Dal Riata, and in the late 7th and early 8th centuries Ferchar Fota and his son Selbach held that position. Selbach burned Dunollie in 701 and later rebuilt it.
cenel-loairn.e: Selbach's defeat at sea in 719 and Pictish conquest under Oengus son of Fergus in the 730s broke Cenel Loairn's power. Later Scottish genealogies traced the rulers of the Kingdom of Moray, including Macbeth, to this kindred, though the link is debated.

county-of-hainaut.t: A cloth and coal county of the southern Low Countries, ruled from Mons for nine centuries and long linked by marriage to Flanders and Holland.
county-of-hainaut.o: Hainaut grew out of a Carolingian district on the Scheldt and Sambre. Around 898 Reginar Longneck, a leading Lotharingian noble, held comital power there, and his descendants, the Reginarids, struggled with the German kings for control. By the 11th century the county was centred on Mons and Valenciennes.
county-of-hainaut.r: Hainaut lay within the Holy Roman Empire but faced France, and its counts played both sides. The marriage of Richilde to Baldwin VI of Flanders in 1051 began a long Flemish link; Baldwin IX of Flanders, count of Hainaut, became the first Latin emperor of Constantinople in 1204. Towns grew rich on cloth, and the countryside later on coal.
county-of-hainaut.e: Hainaut was united with Holland under the Avesnes counts from 1299, and Jacqueline of Bavaria lost both to Philip the Good of the Burgundian State in 1433. The Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678 gave its south to France; the rest stayed in the Spanish Netherlands and Austrian Netherlands until French annexation in 1795.

carthaginiensis.t: The late Roman province of central and south-eastern Hispania, named after its capital Carthago Nova, modern Cartagena.
carthaginiensis.o: Carthaginiensis was created around 293 by Diocletian, who divided Hispania Tarraconensis. It took in the south-east coast and much of the central Meseta, including Toletum, with Carthago Nova as capital. The Balearic Islands belonged to it until about 369.
carthaginiensis.r: A governor administered it within the Diocese of Hispania. Carthago Nova remained a port for esparto, fish sauce and the remains of its silver trade, while inland cities such as Toletum and Complutum grew in importance. Christian communities were well established, and the Council of Elvira of around 305 drew bishops from the region.
carthaginiensis.e: After 409 the Alans and Vandals overran the province, and Roman control was patchy. In 460 the emperor Majorian's fleet, gathered on its coast to attack the Vandals in Africa, was destroyed. The region fell to the Visigoths, and later Byzantine Spania held its coast.

commune-of-viterbo.t: A papal city-commune north of Rome that hosted popes in the 13th century and gave the Church the longest papal election in its history.
commune-of-viterbo.o: Viterbo grew on the Via Cassia in northern Lazio, and consuls governing the town are recorded by 1095. It expanded by subduing neighbouring towns and fought a long rivalry with the Commune of Rome, while recognising the distant overlordship of the Papal States.
commune-of-viterbo.r: The commune was ruled by consuls, then a podestà, while rival clans such as the Gatti and the prefects of Vico fought for control. From the mid-13th century popes often lived there, and the Palazzo dei Papi was built for them. The election of 1268–1271 dragged on for almost three years until the townspeople locked the cardinals in and removed the roof, leading to the conclave rules of Gregory X.
commune-of-viterbo.e: In the 14th century Giovanni di Vico made himself lord of the city until Cardinal Albornoz restored papal authority in 1354. After further strife the town came under direct papal government at the end of the century and remained part of the Papal States until 1870.

cavares.t: Gallic people of the lower Rhône whose towns became Avignon, Cavaillon and Orange.
cavares.o: Strabo names the Cavares as the leading people between the Durance and the Isère, east of the Rhône. Their towns included Avennio (Avignon), Cabellio (Cavaillon) and Arausio (Orange), and they had close commercial ties with Massalia.
cavares.r: Strabo describes them as already largely Romanised in his day. Little is known of their earlier rulers.
cavares.e: They came under Rome after 121 BCE. In 105 BCE the Cimbri and Teutones destroyed two Roman armies at Arausio in their land, one of Rome's worst defeats. Arausio was refounded as a colony for veterans of the Second Legion, with its famous theatre and arch.

caleti.t: Belgic people of the chalk coast of upper Normandy who gave their name to the Pays de Caux.
caleti.o: The Caleti lived on the plateau between the lower Seine and the Channel cliffs. Caesar reports that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
caleti.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Their coast and the Seine estuary gave them a part in cross-Channel trade.
caleti.e: They submitted in 57 BCE but sent men to Alesia in 52 BCE and joined the Bellovaci in 51 BCE. Under Rome their chief town was Juliobona (Lillebonne), whose theatre survives, and the region kept their name as the Pays de Caux.

corieltauvi.t: East Midlands people who issued coins under paired rulers and buried the Hallaton Treasure, and who passed under Roman rule largely without resistance.
corieltauvi.o: The Corieltauvi occupied Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire and parts of the surrounding counties in the late Iron Age; the older name Coritani was corrected after an inscription naming them was found. They grew from local farming communities on the river valleys and wolds, with major centres at Leicester, Old Sleaford and Lincoln.
corieltauvi.r: From the late 1st century BCE they issued gold and silver coins, often with two names together, such as VEP CORF or AVN COST, which may point to joint rule; later issues name Volisios and Dumnocoveros. The Hallaton Treasure, a ritual hoard of more than 5,000 coins and a Roman cavalry helmet, shows close contact with Rome before the conquest. Pottery and iron-working flourished.
corieltauvi.e: The region was occupied soon after 43, apparently with little fighting, and by 47 Roman forts and the legio IX at Lincoln held the area. The people formed the civitas of the Corieltauvi, governed from Ratae Corieltauvorum, modern Leicester, within Roman Britain.

county-of-pallars-jussa.t: The lower half of the Pyrenean county of Pallars, centred on Tremp, which passed to the Crown of Aragon in 1192.
county-of-pallars-jussa.o: When Count Sunyer of Pallars died in 1011, his lands were divided between his sons: Ramon III received the southern, lower part around Tremp and the Noguera Pallaresa valley, while his brother Guillem took the mountainous north, the County of Pallars Sobirà.
county-of-pallars-jussa.r: Pallars Jussà was a frontier county facing the Taifa of Lérida and expanded south by conquest. Its counts were often at odds with their cousins in the north and with the powerful frontier lord Arnau Mir de Tost. Like other Catalan counties, it was organised through castles, feudal oaths and monastic foundations such as Santa Maria de Gerri.
county-of-pallars-jussa.e: In 1192 Countess Dolça bequeathed the county to Alfonso II of Aragon, who incorporated it into the Crown of Aragon. Its lands later formed part of the Principality of Catalonia.

cyzicus.t: Milesian colony on the Sea of Marmara whose electrum coins circulated across the Greek world and which withstood Mithridates in 73 BCE.
cyzicus.o: Cyzicus was founded by Miletus on the isthmus of the Arctonnesus peninsula, on the southern shore of the Propontis; the register follows the date c. 675 BCE, while an earlier foundation c. 756 BCE is also recorded. Its two harbours made it a natural stopping point on the route to the Black Sea.
cyzicus.r: From the 6th century BCE Cyzicus issued electrum staters, the 'Cyzicenes', widely used in trade. It was ruled by the Achaemenid Empire and paid tribute in the Delian League. In 410 BCE Alcibiades destroyed a Spartan fleet off the city. In the Hellenistic period Cyzicus was a close ally of the Kingdom of Pergamon.
cyzicus.e: Cyzicus withstood a long siege by Mithridates in 73 BCE until Lucullus relieved it, and Rome rewarded it as a free city. It lost that status in 20 BCE, regained it, and lost it finally under Tiberius in 25 CE.
